#146414. Pondering The Potential Of Plug-In VPP

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1378 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

Pondering The Potential Of Plug-In VPP

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1378 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I recently discussed the potential of the plug-in VPP from Jackery and Every Electric to transform urban energy storage.
  • Industry observers note that essentially, customers of the plug-in VPP receive a battery, plug it into the wall and their window air conditioner, and connect to Wi-Fi.
  • It has been revealed that both Jackery and Every Electric are collaborating and working to create innovative solutions for customer needs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I recently discussed the potential of the plug-in VPP from Jackery and Every Electric to transform urban energy storage. But the current program could be just the start. The more I discussed it at RE+, the more it started making me thing about where it could go in the future.

Industry observers note that essentially, customers of the plug-in VPP receive a battery, plug it into the wall and their window air conditioner, and connect to Wi-Fi. Then they use AC as they normally would, the VPP shaves off demand peaks on the grid, and the customer gets paid. It is likely the fastest, easiest and cheapest way to implement urban BESS in the US. And regular people living in apartments benefit. You can read more about the plug-in VPP in my previous article for context. Or you can watch the video below.

It has been revealed that both Jackery and Every Electric are collaborating and working to create innovative solutions for customer needs. Plug-in VPP makes the benefits of battery storage accessible to people in apartments. However, the potential could go much farther. Of note, much of what I am discussing here is not available yet. But the plug-in VPP sparked my imagination, and I wanted to expand on what might be possible.

Sources indicate that initially, the system is being deployed in New York City, which has a large number of apartments that can be aggregated to create a meaningful amount of combined storage. Of course, the potential can be realized in areas outside of NYC. Every Electric is already looking to expand into the Boston area. There are several other areas where the existing system based on window air conditioners in urban areas could apply, particularly along the Northeast corridor. However, as the program evolves, there is tremendous potential outside of the region.

Recent findings suggest that in Jackery’s home state of California, 4.5 TWh of solar and wind power was curtailed in the first half of 2026. More electricity wasted in six months in one state than many developing countries consume in an entire year. Residential solar often feeds into the grid when it just leads to curtailments elsewhere. Even with recent ESS installations, the Duck Curve is still deepening. If home batteries can help “decapitate the duck,” customers and the utility both stand to benefit. And all that renewable energy right now being wasted can contribute to reducing emissions.

In addition, every Jackery battery can operate as a solar generator, with a DC input. People can simply plug in a solar panel or two to recharge the battery. No additional inverter needed. As it does not send energy back into the grid, it also avoids the cost and complication of traditional grid-tied systems. Sending solar power directly to the battery would avoid having excess solar generation fed into the grid that contributes to overcapacity, deepening the back of the duck curve. Demand response could then come from a battery charged largely from solar, rather than from the grid. As the US is still trying to figure out balcony solar regulations, this would let people enjoy many of the benefits of small scale, plug-and-play solar now. No electricians needed.

In a recent development, of course, when balcony solar regulations are figured out, Jackery has solutions like the SolarVault3 that I saw at IFA Berlin. Potentially, this system could integrate with point of use battery storage to form a kind of hybrid plug-in system. In the process, solar power could be utilized when it does the most for the grid and offers the greatest potential payback for the customer.

There is also a lot of potential for this concept to work outside of the US. In many parts of the world, most people live in apartments. As the planet warms, world cooling needs recently overtook heating for the first time. As the VPP is monitored via a Wi-Fi connection, there is no need to upgrade to a smart meter to take advantage of the capability. As the storage is already distributed, there is also reduced need to provide the grid upgrades to distribute the energy stored in a large battery during peak energy demand.

Right now, the plug-in VPP is only working with one model of battery in one application. That makes the deployment and scaling of the plug-in VPP easier. Large urban areas offer the clearest path to aggregate the storage needed for a plug-in VPP to work.

However, Jackery has sold over 8 million units over the past 15 years. This has established a level of customer trust and a reputation for reliability. Many of those portable power stations and solar generators can connect to Wi-Fi. That is potentially GWh of deployable storage.

In a recent development, in addition, portable power stations are very popular now. Many Jackery models are selling out. Preparedness is a major driver. Climate-related disasters amplify the fear and uncertainty. However, the batteries that people are buying to be prepared for emergencies offer far greater potential capability. The more batteries that are out there, the greater the potential.

As the software and capability of the VPP develop, multiple batteries have the potential to connect to amplify value, even if that capability isn’t being offered yet. Those batteries, in coordination with a VPP, could earn people money. Currently, the system is being run with one battery model, but Jackery offers a wide range of batteries with Wi-Fi connectivity that might be able to participate in the future. Once the program has proven itself with the initial application in urban areas, there is potential for expansion.

As people start earning money, even if they purchased the battery out of preparedness concerns, they would also start to see the broader benefit. When they gain both confidence and financial benefit from battery storage and renewable energy, they will tend to rationalize that benefit. That can lead to a broader shift in mindset. When you try to start with a rational argument, especially when that argument involves added costs, people are less likely to be supportive than if you start with the benefit.

It has been revealed that many of the pieces to make this happen have already existed. People have the ability to program Jackery batteries through the app to charge and discharge during certain parts of the day. This can work with TOU utility intends, where available. But it doesn’t take full advantage of the capabilities of a VPP. Customers do not get full credit for the storage capability. The true innovation comes from putting the pieces together, between the Jackery hardware, Every Electric software and the utility. If one of those pieces of the collaboration was missing, a plug-in VPP wouldn’t have the same potential.

One of the things that has impressed me about Jackery since I was first introduced to the manufacturer was their focus on solving customer problems. However, to create solutions, they also recognize that collaboration is often necessary. I already saw this with the flexible solar panels of SunBooster at IFA Berlin for balcony solar applications, and then again with Every Electric for plug-in VPP.

I asked Jackery founder and CEO Jack Sun about the value of collaboration in creating an environmentally friendly ecosystem:.

This is also very important, because we have an open model, and we are more willing and more innovative….

We will actively collaborate with partners in areas such as power chips and more proactively in co-creation. We aim to accelerate the application of their innovations into our solar generator solutions. Our goal is to achieve faster and more efficient solar energy development through joint innovation. The generator can be installed in every household to help more families achieve energy independence more cost-effectively, while also reducing carbon emissions more quickly.

This focus on collaboration makes meaningful innovation happen. Just as I speculated here on the potential of plug-in VPP, other people will have their own ideas. Some will be different than this VPP concept. Many will be better ideas than the ideas I can come up with. Having innovative companies like Jackery and Every Electric actively seeking to work with partners creates potential for those ideas to come together. I look forward to seeing what new solutions come together next.

US to install 36% more wind turbines in 2025 than previous year

📅 18 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Windpowerengineering

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the United States is expected to add more than 7 GW of wind installations in 2025, a 36% increase over the previous year, and the five-year outlook remains unchanged quarter-over-quarter from previous forecast, according to the “U.S.
  • In a recent development, amid a challenging market environment, the report reveals that the United States is on track to add 46 GW of upcoming wind capacity from 2025 to 2029, with total projected volumes unchanged quarter-on-quarter from previous forecasts.
  • While Q3 installations came in 23% below forecast at 932 MW, the market has shown progress with 3.8 GW queued for Q4 2025 — representing 52% of the year’s total expected capacity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the United States is expected to add more than 7 GW of wind installations in 2025, a 36% increase over the previous year, and the five-year outlook remains unchanged quarter-over-quarter from previous forecast, according to the “U.S. Wind Energy Monitor” report released by Wood Mackenzie and the American Clean Power Association (ACP).

In a recent development, amid a challenging market environment, the report reveals that the United States is on track to add 46 GW of upcoming wind capacity from 2025 to 2029, with total projected volumes unchanged quarter-on-quarter from previous forecasts. However, timing has shifted, as 2026 and 2027 will deliver significant gains, at 10.7 GW and 12.7 GW, respectively, as more assets advance through the development pipeline.

While Q3 installations came in 23% below forecast at 932 MW, the market has shown progress with 3.8 GW queued for Q4 2025 — representing 52% of the year’s total expected capacity. This back-loaded installation pattern is consistent with typical project-commissioning timelines.

U.S. turbine order intake has rebounded to pre-One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) levels quarter-over-quarter, supported by 2+ GW of firm commitments in Q3, the biggest intake in the region in the last nine months and a 79% quarter-over-quarter increase. However, true visibility remains limited as OEMs increasingly withhold project details and much qualifying “start-of-construction” activity occurs through off-site component manufacturing.

The market will then see a noticeable drop off, as 2029 weakens meaningfully quarter-over-quarter following project cancellations and inactive designations for late-decade capacity, driven by permitting and broader development challenges.

In a recent development, “The U.S. power market is facing mounting strain after a decade of flat demand, with utilities committing to 160 GW of large-load additions. This represents a significant opportunity for wind energy, which benefits from strengthened economic fundamentals and a compelling business case driven by its competitively low LCOE,” said Leila Garcia da Fonseca, director of research at Wood Mackenzie. “However, turbine costs remain elevated due to tariffs and mid-term wind growth will depend on resolving permitting and policy uncertainty.”.

Sources indicate that power demand growth through 2029 is expected to average around 3% compared to just 0.7% over the previous decade, with data centers accounting for approximately 59 GW of the 90 GW total peak demand growth. This surge in baseload demand positions wind as a natural fit to meet rising power needs.

According to recent reports, the five-year capacity outlook remains unchanged at 39.8 GW of added capacity quarter-over-quarter. The 2025-2027 pipeline is fully committed with all projects having turbine orders in place. More than 60% of the three-year capacity outlook has been commissioned or is under construction.

Activity is led by western states, such as Wyoming, New Mexico and others, that will account for 34% of activity in this time period. Major projects driving the outlook include Pattern’s 3.5-GW SunZia project in New Mexico, which will position the developer as 2026’s top installer, and Invenergy’s 998-MW Towner Energy Center in Colorado, the largest single project expected in 2027.

The market continues expanding geographically, with Arkansas bringing its first utility-scale onshore wind project online through Cordelio’s Crossover Wind.

The repowering market remains strong, as Wood Mackenzie projects that 18 projects will drive 2.5 GW of capacity additions in the next three years.

Wood Mackenzie expects the offshore installation pace to slow in Q4 2025 due to harsh winter weather conditions, pushing remaining capacity into 2026. Despite these near-term adjustments, Vineyard Wind has demonstrated strong execution, connecting 15 turbines in Q3 and delivering 200 GWh through nine months.

“U.S. offshore wind shows diverging momentum,” said Garcia Da Fonseca. “Projects under construction with COD estimated for 2026 continue to hit key milestones, but post-2027 developments face potential delays amid constrained wind turbine installation vessel capacity, driving delays and contract terminations.”.

The offshore sector is also experiencing significant financial pressure.

The report highlights that uncertainty around tariffs is a threat to projections. Wood Mackenzie projects that tariffs will drive up turbine costs in 2026, before moderating in subsequent years. In total, U.S. onshore wind capex is projected to increase by 5% through 2029.

“U.S. wind turbine pricing is experiencing unprecedented uncertainty as conflicting market and regulatory forces interact,” mentioned Garcia Da Fonseca. “Domestic manufacturing overcapacity relative to permitted project volumes, particularly after 2028, would normally place downward pressure on prices. Despite this, onshore wind costs are expected to continue rising due to tariff exposure on raw material inputs and subcomponents.”.

Groups Respond to Army’s Initiative to Proceed with Lead Azide Detonation in Iowa

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, army indicates it plans to detonate degraded lead in Iowa town no later than Nov.
  • Des Moines, IOWA — The Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club, and Earthjustice will continue to advocate for accountability from the U.S.
  • Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a statement with the court late on Saturday, Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, army indicates it plans to detonate degraded lead in Iowa town no later than Nov. 24, despite court stay.

Des Moines, IOWA — The Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club, and Earthjustice will continue to advocate for accountability from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the U.S. Army in the planned detonation of lead azide in Middletown, Iowa. Early Sunday morning, the groups filed declarations with the court that call out the Army’s inadequate public notice and information, and question the Army’s and EPA’s claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration.

It has been revealed that the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) filed a statement with the court late on Saturday, Nov. 21, indicating that the Army intends to invoke emergency provisions of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) to detonate 9,773.5 pounds of lead azide stored at the Iowa Army Ammunitions Plant, without a permit from the EPA. According to the DOJ’s court filings, the Army intends to do so no later than Nov. 24. On Nov. 20, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals granted Earthjustice’s request to put on hold a permit allowing the Army to detonate.

According to recent reports, “People across numerous impacted communities speaking up and demanding accountability is the only reason there was an opportunity to pause and think about better ways to approach the lead azide problem,” said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau. “Yet despite claiming public safety is its top priority and public communication is essential to trust, the Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public’s demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm.”.

In a recent development, this emergency is of the Army’s own making. The Army has not publicly provided details about why the lead azide was not disposed of before it became so dangerous. The Army’s own storage and inspection practices allowed a primary explosive to sit until it reportedly degraded to the point that any alternative disposal method is now deemed too dangerous. The lack of transparency raises real questions about the scope and extent of potential impacts.

“The new information from the DOJ indicates that the problem is significantly worse than the Army originally shared. It appears that detonation may be, at this point, the only feasible option due to how long this problem was allowed to persist. The public deserves to know immediately which communities will be impacted and how residents can most effectively protect themselves and mitigate impacts on their health and homes,” said Michael Schmidt, General Counsel for the Iowa Environmental Council.

According to recent reports, the Army knew about this stockpile of dangerous munitions waste for years, and it knew since at least March that the material was becoming unstable. Yet, just one week ago, most Iowans — including those directly in the path of a toxic lead plume, the Iowa governor, and key state agencies and officials — were unaware the Army intended to detonate nearly five tons of lead azide.

The environmental groups argue the EPA and Army permitting documents have not demonstrated, nor provided appropriate documentation that all other safer alternatives to mitigate the material were thoroughly explored.

“The Army has clearly mishandled this situation, and Iowans and residents in our neighboring states deserve a full review of all of the missteps that led us to this point. However, if detonation is now the only option, it is imperative that everyone impacted has access to the full range of testing, mitigation, and remediation resources,” said Wally Taylor, Attorney and Legal Chair for the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter.

In a recent development, as of 11 a.m. CST on Sunday, Nov. 22, the Army has failed to provide the public with updated weather modeling and mapping showing the path of the lead dust plume, which means people impacted have little time to take precautions to protect their families and homes. The wind patterns have shifted significantly, which means that potential community exposures have likely changed without visible effort by the Army to provide updated information to the public.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jessica Alba’s divorce from Cash Warren is back in the headlines after a upcoming court order awarded Warren $577,481 from Alba’s retirement benefits.

The ruling comes after the former couple sold their longtime Beverly Hills–area home and Alba later purchased another property in the area.

The retirement award comes from Alba’s account in the HonorBar Inc. Profit Sharing Strategy, according to court documents reported by TMZ.

In a recent development, any money left in the account after Warren receives his share is to go to Alba. The documents also allow Warren to take the award as a lump sum or move it into an individual retirement account or another retirement strategy.

The court order also addresses account records: If Warren requests statements in writing within the next year, Alba must provide them within 10 days.

According to the outlet, transferring the money into a retirement account could avoid a 20% tax withholding.

The ruling is the latest financial development following the couple’s divorce, which was finalized in February 2026.

It was previously reported that Alba was ordered to pay Warren $3 million to balance the division of their assets.

Their settlement also divided interests in several companies, shares in The Honest Company, and residuals from projects made during their marriage.

Meanwhile, Alba and Warren have already put their real estate ties behind them.

In a recent development, their former Beverly Hills–area home was sold in 2025. Alba and Warren purchased the seven-bedroom estate for $9.9 million in 2017, then put it on the market in April 2025 for $18.99 million. It was sold for $18.2 million, with the closing recorded on June 27, 2025.

The property sat on about 1.86 acres and included 8.5 bathrooms, a guesthouse, a home theater, and extensive grounds.

Alba and Warren undertook an 18-month renovation after buying it, with Alba involved in decisions about the home’s design.

The estate had been a family residence for years, and Alba spoke about the family’s prepares for the house during a 2019 Architectural Digest tour.

After the sale, Alba picked up a splashy Beverly Hills estate in September 2025 for $4.75 million.

The roughly 5,000-square-foot property boasts four bedrooms, five bathrooms, tiled roofing, and modern amenities.

The two transactions mark a change in Alba’s recent housing history: the end of her and Warren’s ownership of a sprawling family estate, followed by her purchase of another Beverly Hills property.

Alba and Warren revealed their separation in December 2024 after 16 years of marriage.

Alba filed for divorce citing irreconcilable differences, and the sale of their longtime home followed the announcement.

The latest retirement-benefit order concerns a separate part of their financial settlement, while the Beverly Hills transactions provide a look at the real estate changes that accompanied their split.

#146396. Industry News: Barcelona Is Suffering From The Hydrogen Transport Death Spiral

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (892 w)

Industry News: Barcelona Is Suffering From The Hydrogen Transport Death Spiral

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on November 21, Barcelona had at least 23 of its 46 hydrogen buses out of service because the plant supplying them had stopped producing fuel.
  • The problem runs through a single industrial fuel supply.
  • It has been revealed that la Vanguardia connected the Barcelona stoppage with Cummins’ recommendation that customers stop using affected electrolysers following a safety review.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on November 21, Barcelona had at least 23 of its 46 hydrogen buses out of service because the plant supplying them had stopped producing fuel. Transports Metropolitans de Barcelona (TMB) reported a 2.5% to 3.8% reduction in scheduled bus service, with waits on some routes rising from seven to nine minutes. The buses were available to carry passengers. The hydrogen was not. ARA and La Vanguardia reported the disruption.

The problem runs through a single industrial fuel supply. TMB has a ten-year, €14.5 million hydrogen contract with Iberdrola. Alternative deliveries from Tarragona have fallen short, disrupted by industrial action and restrictions on hydrogen transport. The contract provides for compensation when fuel is not delivered. It cannot make up the missed service.

It has been revealed that la Vanguardia connected the Barcelona stoppage with Cummins’ recommendation that customers stop using affected electrolysers following a safety review. Iberdrola cited a valve-system problem at the plant. Cummins’ November quarterly filing confirmed the September HyLYZER stop-use recommendation and mentioned no formal recall had been initiated. TMB now has to assess the price of safely restarting fuel production and the reliability of the system it would be restarting.

Barcelona has not decided to retire the hydrogen buses. But the agency has a more important decision than repairing a plant: whether it should commit public money to keeping this fuel system in service for the remainder of the buses’ lives. Other European cities have faced that choice and walked away.

Industry observers note that aberdeen paid approximately £13.9 million for 25 hydrogen double-deckers that entered service in 2021. Hydrogen supply problems stranded the fleet in July 2024. After prolonged efforts to restore the operation, the city decided in February 2026 to dispose of the buses. A proposed sale would bring in £30,000 each for 23 buses going to First Bus and £63,000 each for two going to GeoPura. The total expected proceeds are £816,000, just 5.9% of the original vehicle expenditure. My September Aberdeen resale assessment examined the proposed terms and the conversion economics. First Bus has also considered battery-electric conversion.

In a recent development, liverpool chose conversion. Ten of its 20 hydrogen buses had never carried passengers; the other ten had completed only 450 passenger-carrying journeys. In December 2025 the Liverpool City Region Combined Authority decided to convert all 20 to battery-electric operation, with the supplier covering the conversion costs. The buses had years of potential mechanical life, but the hydrogen supply arrangements had not delivered a usable transport service.

A hydrogen bus can become an uneconomic asset long before it wears out. Refuelling plants, fuel deliveries, maintenance specialists, software, fuel-cell modules and replacement parts have to remain available. As hydrogen fleets retire and upcoming orders thin out, each remaining operator has fewer other customers sharing those support costs. Rising costs and uncertain service then encourage another operator to exit. That is the hydrogen transport death spiral. Battery-electric buses draw on a much larger manufacturing, charging and maintenance market.

Sources indicate that the pressures already extend through the supply chain. Cummins has stopped seeking newly introduced commercial electrolyser business while customers contend with its HyLYZER stop-use recommendation. Quantron’s insolvency disrupted confidence in specialist vehicle support. Alstom acquired Cummins’ relevant rail fuel-cell operations to retain the staff and expertise needed to fulfil long-term contracts. Each case transfers more risk to organizations that have already bought hydrogen equipment.

Industry observers note that new Flyer still sells hydrogen buses, but the North American order book is thin. Publicly identified hydrogen-bus orders numbered 288 in 2023, 96 in 2024 and no more than 45 gross in 2025, with about 15 in a stricter reconstruction. Another 38 buses appear in 2026 procurement decisions across differing approval stages. These are small volumes for a specialist vehicle line that needs engineering, spares and continuing product development.

Ballard is still developing bus fuel cells. Its November 5 Solaris announcement describes a fresh engine entering series production. Its GeoPura acquisition also shifts business attention toward integrated power systems and recurring energy-service revenue. My Ballard–New Flyer framework assessment found that the March agreement covering 500 modules is not an order for 500 buses. For a transit operator, the crucial test is a binding, affordable commitment to parts, diagnostics and maintenance throughout the vehicles’ remaining service lives.

Recent findings suggest that TMB should compare the cost of safely restarting the hydrogen plant and running the buses with the cost of delivering the same passenger service through replacement vehicles. That includes the repair bill, future fuel contracts, station maintenance, spare parts, service interruptions, replacement buses, depot charging and any temporary vehicles required to keep routes operating. TMB already runs battery-electric buses and has local operating data to test a replacement plan.

A modest repair may justify running the existing hydrogen buses while alternatives are prepared. A major refurbishment, fresh fuel commitments and another decade of specialist support are a different investment. Aberdeen chose disposal. Liverpool chose conversion. Barcelona needs to decide what delivers dependable bus service at the lowest credible forward cost, without treating the original hydrogen spending as money it can recover.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines the Barcelona interruption, the Aberdeen and Liverpool exits, and the contracting support market. The paid section sets out how transit boards can compare restarting, bridging and retiring an existing hydrogen fleet.

Dominion Energy released the following statement in response to the pause issued for the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project:.

“The Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project (CVOW) is essential for American national security and meeting Virginia’s dramatically growing energy needs, the fastest growth in America. This growth is driven by the need to provide reliable power to many of America’s most notable war fighting installations, the world’s largest warship manufacturer, and the largest concentration of data centers on the planet as well as the leading edge of the AI revolution.

Stopping CVOW for any length of time will threaten grid reliability for some of the nation’s most key war fighting, AI and civilian assets. It will also lead to energy inflation and threaten thousands of jobs.

Industry observers note that CVOW is American-owned and benefits all of our Virginia customers. Our customers are paying for the project after a careful review of project costs and benefits by Virginia state regulators in 2022. These same state regulators, along with numerous federal agencies, oversee our cyber and physical security program, which is among the strongest in the energy industry.

The project has been more than 10 years in the works, involved close coordination with the military, and is located 27 to 44 miles offshore, so far offshore it does not raise visual impact concerns. The project’s two pilot turbines have been operating for five years without causing any impacts to national security.

Industry observers note that CVOW enjoys bipartisan support and is within months of generating a massive 2,600 MW to support the fastest growing part of America’s energy grid. This growth serves the largest concentration of critical infrastructure in the world.

Sources indicate that virginia’s All-American, All-Of-The-Above-Energy Initiative requires a range of power generation assets, including natural gas, advanced nuclear, and renewables. Virginia needs every electron we can get as our demand for electricity doubles. These electrons will power the data centers that will win the AI race, support our war fighters, and build the nuclear warships needed to maintain our maritime supremacy. Virginia’s grid needs addition of electrons, not subtraction.

We stand ready to do what is necessary to get these vital electrons flowing as quickly as possible.”.

#146391. COP31 Plants A Major Wet Kiss On Failed Carbon Capture Technology

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

COP31 Plants A Major Wet Kiss On Failed Carbon Capture Technology

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1213 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • COP31, the annual UN climate conference that took place this month, ended on a sour note after negotiators were unable to reach an agreement to include language calling for a transition away from fossil fuels in the final communiqué  — language that was included two years ago at the conclusion of COP 29 in Dubai.
  • Sources indicate that how is it possible to explain such backsliding at a time when a Kelvin wave — a wall of unusually hot water — is impacting the coast of every country along the eastern edge of the Pacific Ocean?
  • It has been revealed that you know the answer — MONEY!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

COP31, the annual UN climate conference that took place this month, ended on a sour note after negotiators were unable to reach an agreement to include language calling for a transition away from fossil fuels in the final communiqué  — language that was included two years ago at the conclusion of COP 29 in Dubai.

Sources indicate that how is it possible to explain such backsliding at a time when a Kelvin wave — a wall of unusually hot water — is impacting the coast of every country along the eastern edge of the Pacific Ocean? Authorities say unusually high temperatures all across Europe led to the premature death of more than 50,000 people last summer. In addition, huge swaths of the Earth’s land mass are experiencing either severe drought or punishing floods. How can anybody ignore the events happening before their very eyes?

It has been revealed that you know the answer — MONEY! According to Kathryn McCallum, the director of strategy at the Climate Action Network Australia, there were 624 delegates from the 14 Pacificc Small Island Developing States at the conference in Turkey this month and 700 paid lobbyists for the carbon capture industry. In an email to CleanTechnica, she said,.

In a recent development, “There is no public momentum from parties in the COP31 process asking for carbon capture, utilization and storage, yet it is in the final draft text. As a result, in the coming hours, parties at COP31 will decide whether to lock in a [methane] fired future with a rapid scale-up of carbon dumping. The potential inclusion of a huge increase in global carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) would be one of the biggest loopholes for the fossil fuel industry ever to be included in a COP text. Climate advocates are highly alarmed and are urging parties to come to their senses and make decisions that advance global climate action rather than the interests of the gas industry.”.

Recent findings suggest that as it turns out, the knife in the back delivered by fossil fuel interests at COP31 was too much for negotiators from the EU and the UK to swallow. According to reNEWS, the European Union expressed its “profound disappointment” with the draft cover decision following the close of the COP31 conference.

According to recent reports, “At a point where the world urgently needs action to avert disastrous level of global warming, the draft cover decision falls short,” a joint EU statement read. “We will not endorse a cover decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5°C within reach. We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change.”.

The statement listed a number on other concerns with the draft cover decision, including that the draft extols carbon capture, usage, and storage technologies “disproportionally” as a method to deal with the climate crisis. This is magical thinking, the statement by the EU mentioned.

It has been revealed that the UK also refused to be sucked in by the absurd claims that carbon capture was a plausible alternative to reducing the world’s reliance on fossil fuels. The Independent reports that UK energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh expressed regret that the talks had failed to produce the “bold ambition” needed, as the negotiations became mired in disagreement over a draft agreement that contained no mention of fossil fuels.

Sources indicate that the UK formally objected to a proposed deal that “moves us backwards on the science” of tackling climate change. In a statement, Fahnbulleh noted, “This COP sought to confront hard truths — that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with ever more urgency to address it. The moment required bold ambition and we have been working tirelessly to try to build consensus. It is immensely disappointing we have been unable to do so.”.

Recent findings suggest that there are a number of ways to remediate the emissions from burning fossil fuels, which are nothing more than stored sunshine from millions of years ago. We could irradiate them with unicorn farts, incinerate them in nuclear fusion facilities, are store them in the basement at Mar-A-Loco, where large quantities of toxic fumes are already present. There is only one problem — none of those solutions work. In fact, the only thing that does work is burning less fossil fuels, until we are able to phase them out entirely.

Industry observers note that in  2025, Mark Jacobson, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at Stanford University, and his colleagues, published a research paper in the journal Environmental Science and Technology. In it he wrote that if the nations of the world transitioned to renewable energy — solar, wind, and hydroelectric power — they would eliminate energy-related air pollution deaths and CO2-equivalent emissions while reducing their energy needs by 54.4 percent, annual energy costs by 59.6 percent, and annual social costs — energy, plus health, plus climate — by 91.8 percent. Who wouldn’t want that?

Sources indicate that on the other hand, Jacobson and his team wrote that every dollar spent on carbon capture instead of wind, water, and solar, “increases carbon dioxide pollution, energy requirements, energy costs, pipelines, and total social costs.” This holds true even if zero-emission energy systems power the technology deployed to extract carbon dioxide. “It’s always an opportunity cost to use clean, renewable energy for direct air capture instead of replacing a fossil fuel CO2 source, just like it’s an opportunity cost to use it for AI or bitcoin mining. You’re preventing renewables from replacing fossil fuel sources because you’re creating more demand for those renewables,” he noted.

It has been revealed that “Opportunity costs” is the operative concept here. If you are in Peoria, you cannot be in Philadelphia. If you spend $10.00 on pretzels, you cannot spend it on vegetables. If you buy a new car, you cannot use that money to go to Cabo San Lucas. The money the world pisses away on carbon capture cannot be used to build solar, wind, and hydro resources. It’s as simple as that.

The take away here is that fossil fuels will always win the policy debate. So what will drive the transition to renewable energy? Lower prices for renewables and eliminating concerns about energy insecurity from geopolitical disruptions like the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Low prices always win and people are pretty sick and tired of paying six bucks for diesel while watching the cost of electricity soar higher and higher.

“The first one now shall later be last,” Bob Dylan taught us. That’s a message of hope inside the carbon dioxide cloud the fossil fuel industry has gifted us. The only question is whether the transition will happen soon enough to avoid a climate catastrophe. It’s hard to imagine destroying a planet and decimating your customer base is a good long term business strategy, but that’s what the executives in charge of the world’s oil, methane, and coal industries seem to think makes for good business. There are none so blind as those who will not see.

The European Competitiveness Fund, the Backbone of a Modern European Investment Policy

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • European businesses call for a robust, well-funded European Competitiveness Fund.
  • Europe is losing ground in technological leadership and struggles to scale strategic technologies, while volatile energy costs and external dependencies continue to dampen business confidence.
  • According to recent reports, europe’s path to enduring technological leadership relies on our ability to scale strategic technologies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

European businesses call for a robust, well-funded European Competitiveness Fund.

Dear Chancellors, Prime Ministers, Presidents,.

Europe is losing ground in technological leadership and struggles to scale strategic technologies, while volatile energy costs and external dependencies continue to dampen business confidence.

According to recent reports, europe’s path to enduring technological leadership relies on our ability to scale strategic technologies. By stabilising energy costs, providing a path to clean industrial renewal and cultivating European resilience, we are laying the groundwork for robust business and investors’ confidence. Public investment has a crucial role to play to address these vital challenges. We require a smarter, more strategic investment policy for Europe.

We, more than 75 undersigned businesses, call on European leaders to agree to a Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) commensurate with Europe’s challenges, to protect its investment capacity and place long-term productivity growth, resilience and decarbonisation at its core. We believe the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF) represents a step-change in the EU’s investment policy and must be strengthened in the remaining negotiations.

It has been revealed that the ECF with its toolbox projects the ambition to provide tailored support to the investment and scale-up challenge Europe faces. This is a positive evolution of the EU funding landscape. With a bigger role for the EU’s derisking instrument InvestEU, the ECF can become Europe’s modern investment vehicle with an increased use of guarantees, loans and equity to unlock strategic investments.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, non-repayable support needs to be dedicated to scaling up sectors that deliver high strategic value but cannot yet secure commercial capital in Europe. Ramp-up support for Europe’s cleantech manufacturing, including support for OpEx, is needed to make Europe’s bid to regain technological leadership credible.

The advisory services for SMEs and the single access portal promises a simpler access to funding for firms across Europe. If successful, the ECF can pool additional national funds through merit-based procedures open to eligible projects across the single market to bring further alignment and synergies into European industrial development.

Europe’s energy import dependency has become a strategic vulnerability for European businesses. To increase our economic resilience, the EU must prioritise investments into energy sovereignty. Incentives need to pivot capital allocation away from fossil fuel infrastructure, and towards clean energy and electrification. From 2028, the next MFF should not support upcoming fossil-fuel infrastructure that prolongs dependency on fossil fuels, while providing narrowly defined safeguards for security of supply. We need steering mechanisms to reduce fossil fuel dependencies. EU funding can help to tackle high upfront costs and derisk the switch to cleaner and more reliable energy. Otherwise, long investment cycles create severe fossil fuel lock-in effects that threaten our operational autonomy with increasingly volatile fossil energy prices.

Recent findings suggest that europe’s investment gap cannot be solved by a smarter, more strategic funding approach alone. The confidence into European competitiveness needs to translate into a sizable budget for the clean transition to have lasting impact. The Commission proposes an average annual budget of €3.3 billion for a clean transition and industrial decarbonisation window of the ECF. This number is dwarfed by recurring estimates of the annual climate investment deficit of €344 billion. At the same time, according to the OECD, industrial subsidies have reached the highest levels since the financial crisis 2008.

We urge European leaders to respond to the evolving investment environment and adopt the European Parliament’s proposal to increase the size of the ECF by €26.6 billion and to allocate a substantial share of the additional funding for industrial decarbonisation and clean transition. The more efficient use of financial instruments and a strategic prioritisation can improve the impact of EU funding but cannot substitute the investment needs Europe is facing to boost competitiveness and security.

Sources indicate that the next long-term budget and the European Competitiveness Fund must become the investment trigger for European businesses to regain competitiveness at the global scale, based on clear incentives and regulatory certainty. We businesses urge leaders to demonstrate a long-term vision and make the ECF the cornerstone of a new EU green industrial strategy.

Download the letter to see the full list of signatories.

#146384. Smarter Cooling, Stronger Reliability: Advancing Wind Turbine Gearbox Performance

📅 23 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1021 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Windpowerengineering ↗ Open Full Page

Smarter Cooling, Stronger Reliability: Advancing Wind Turbine Gearbox Performance

📅 23 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Windpowerengineering

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the wind energy industry matures, operators and service providers are increasingly focused on maximizing turbine availability while controlling long-term maintenance costs.
  • Heat exchangers play a critical role in maintaining proper oil temperature and viscosity within wind turbine gearboxes.
  • “Wind operators today are balancing increasing performance expectations with the realities of aging fleets and rising maintenance costs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the wind energy industry matures, operators and service providers are increasingly focused on maximizing turbine availability while controlling long-term maintenance costs. Although major drivetrain components often receive the spotlight, one overlooked system can have an outsized impact on turbine reliability and performance: gearbox oil cooling.

Heat exchangers play a critical role in maintaining proper oil temperature and viscosity within wind turbine gearboxes. When cooling systems become clogged with airborne debris, dust, or organic material, oil temperatures rise, lubrication performance declines, and component stress increases. Over time, these conditions can contribute to reduced gearbox efficiency, elevated maintenance demands, and avoidable downtime.

“Wind operators today are balancing increasing performance expectations with the realities of aging fleets and rising maintenance costs. Technologies that improve cooling efficiency and reduce service exposure can have a meaningful impact on long-term turbine reliability and operational profitability,” according to Mike Erickson, HYDAC’s Market Manager for the Wind Industry.

It has been revealed that traditional “panel cut” heat exchanger designs have long been susceptible to clogging due to their tightly packed fin structures. In many wind environments — particularly agricultural, dusty, or high-pollen regions — debris accumulation can severely restrict airflow. Oil leaks can further compound the concern by trapping contaminants within the exchanger core, making cleaning more difficult and labor intensive.

This operational challenge has driven the need for more resilient cooling technologies designed specifically for real-world wind farm conditions.

HYDAC’s newly introduced “Square Wave” heat exchanger design represents a significant advancement in addressing these reliability concerns. Engineered to allow debris to pass more freely through the exchanger fins, the design minimizes clogging while improving cooling efficiency under demanding operating conditions.

The importance of effective cooling cannot be overstated. Wind turbine gearbox oil typically operates within an optimal temperature range of approximately 45°C to 65°C. Even modest temperature increases can significantly impact oil viscosity. According to field data, a 12°C rise in oil temperature can reduce viscosity by nearly 28 percent — affecting lubrication quality and accelerating wear on critical drivetrain components.

According to recent reports, field trials have demonstrated measurable operational benefits from the Square Wave design. During a one-year trial on GE 1.x turbines, the upgraded exchanger consistently reduced clogging and lowered maintenance requirements compared to traditional panel cut cores. Operators reported reduced up-tower cleaning time and fewer temperature-related cooling faults.

According to recent reports, field validation across multiple turbine platforms has further reinforced the operational advantages of the Square Wave design. In one case study involving legacy 1 MW-class turbines operating in the Pacific Northwest, a major renewable energy operator installed pilot sets of Square Wave heat exchangers as part of a cooling performance evaluation. Installation teams reported the upgraded exchangers integrated seamlessly into the existing platform with no retrofit complications.

After initial operating data demonstrated improved cooling consistency, the operator expanded the evaluation program with additional units. Long-term SCADA analysis later highlighted turbines equipped with Square Wave technology operate approximately 20 to 25 percent cooler than comparable turbines using conventional heat exchanger designs under similar operating conditions. The data also highlighted another important advantage: the Square Wave cores continued to maintain airflow and cooling efficiency in debris-heavy environments where traditional exchanger designs became increasingly restricted over time.

The successful deployment also generated interest from additional wind service organizations seeking retrofit-ready cooling upgrades that could improve turbine reliability while reducing maintenance burdens across aging fleets.

DTE Energy recently announced plans to add up to 150 megawatts of new solar energy in Michigan, a move that will create construction jobs, support local communities, and save customers money on fuel costs, the company said.

In addition, because solar generation does not require fuel, the latest projects will help reduce the tech giant’s exposure to changing fuel prices over their operating lives. The projects will also support DTE’s work to provide customers with energy that is reliable, increasingly clean, and affordable.

Industry observers note that the organization stated that these projects are an investment in Michigan and its communities. By producing more Michigan-made energy that doesn’t require the purchase  of fuel, it can help lower energy costs for customers and reduce the reliance on fuel from outside the state. At the same time, these projects will create jobs and bring new investment and tax revenue into local communities, providing more resources for schools, first responders and the services Michigan families count on every day.

DTE is seeking competitive proposals for up to 150 megawatts of newly introduced Michigan-based solar generation. The procurement supports the requirements of the settlement agreement in Michigan Public Service Commission Case No. U-21662, approved May 15, 2025.

Projects must achieve commercial operation by June 30, 2030, be located in Michigan and connect to either the MISO transmission system or DTE’s distribution system. Interested bidders can register and obtain additional information through PowerAdvocate. Proposals are due Jan. 19, 2027, and DTE expects to execute contracts in the second or third quarter of 2027.

Industry observers note that DTE is a producer of and investor in renewable energy in Michigan, generating enough clean energy from wind and solar to power nearly one million homes. As the firm works toward net zero carbon emissions, it remains committed to growing its renewable energy portfolio while maintaining a balanced mix of energy resources that supports reliability and affordability for customers. DTE’s 2026 Integrated Resource Plan builds on that commitment, calling for an additional 15 gigawatts of renewable energy by 2042.

The Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” takes place in the Theranos founder’s former Del Mar, CA, rental—and the property’s location in an exclusive, gated community could be just part of the reason the film’s unexpected release was such a smash.

In a recent development, the project—which is now available to stream on demand and was directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim—was kept secret for the four years it was in production, leaving viewers in awe after the documentary’s surprise Sept. 6 premiere at Telluride Film Festival.

Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, invited the film crew—which Oppenheim told Variety was intentionally kept intimate to keep the project a secret—to reside in the guesthouse of the home for the 34 days before she reported to Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, TX, on May 30, 2023.

“Keeping it under wraps was very notable because we never wanted to get in front of what we were capturing,” the director shared.

The crew would typically shoot for 16-hour days, with Fielder telling Variety that cameras were strategically positioned to “cover the whole house” so nothing would be missed.

In a recent development, the four-bedroom, four-bathroom beachfront property is located in an ultraprivate community less than a half-hour from San Diego. Called Sandy Lane, it features just about a dozen residences.

In a recent development, “This is basically a hidden community. It’s a guard-gated community, which is so rare on a beach, which is why you have a lot of high-profile individuals up and down this strip,” celebrity real estate agent Josh Altman explained in a home tour of another property on the community’s sole street.

Given the home's private location—and considering California’s anti-paparazzi legislation protecting private property from capture—it’s plain to see why Holmes and Evans opted to rent the 2,200-square-foot dwelling in the time leading up to her imprisonment.

Sources indicate that the Fresh York Times also previously reported that the couple and their two children moved to the area to be nearer to Evans’ family. His parents, William L. Evans and Susan Evans, are the hotel magnates behind Evans Hotels, a San Diego–based hospitality manufacturer.

Although the property is at the moment off-market, a previous listing indicates the single-story home was built in 1948 and includes direct access to the private beach.

Sources indicate that as seen in the film, the abode features tall ceilings with exposed-beams and sizable windows connecting the home to the serene surrounding landscape. Midcentury modern design is present throughout the home, which is paneled in honey-hued wood.

Industry observers note that while Realtor.com® estimates the property’s current market value to be about $5.8 million, it’s unclear just how much Holmes and Evans shelled out to reside there temporarily. The most recent publicly listed rent was $5,650 a month in 2015, which is a decrease from the $5,950 rent it was listed for in 2012.

Sources indicate that the Sandy Lane spot is not the only prominent rental property Holmes has retreated to since her legal troubles began. During her trial from Aug. 31, 2021, to Jan. 3, 2022, she resided in one of the seven homes of San Francisco’s notable Green Gables.

The sprawling 74-acre property was owned by the Fleishhacker family for over a century before it was sold for a record-breaking $85 million in 2025.

Before Theranos came crumbling down, Holmes and her former business and romantic partner, Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, purchased a $9 million French provincial manor in Atherton, a wealthy enclave of Silicon Valley.

Privacy was likely a factor in that decision, as well, as the five-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom mansion was set behind a gated entrance and tall trees.

The home was considerably more lavish than the beach bungalow that serves as the backdrop for “You Can See Everything,” with a 6,800-square-foot main home accompanied by gardens, a pool, and a pavilion on a 1.16-acre lot.

Along with the couple’s young children, Evans has since relocated from California to Texas, so the family can visit Holmes in prison, where she is serving an 11-year sentence for three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

The sentence was reduced to nine years for good behavior, and Holmes has since been approved for placement in a community correction center, ABC News reported, citing an patch from the Department of Justice's Victim Notification System.

Holmes is scheduled to be placed in the Austin Transitional Center in De Valle, TX, in August 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Army intends to detonate 9,700 pounds of a lead-based explosive in Southeast Iowa on Wednesday, despite concerns from environmental groups.
  • According to recent reports, the U.S.
  • The controlled detonated of the country's entire stockpile of the explosive was carried out at at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, IA at 10am EST.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Army intends to detonate 9,700 pounds of a lead-based explosive in Southeast Iowa on Wednesday, despite concerns from environmental groups.

According to recent reports, the U.S. army has detonated 9,7000 pounds of a lead-based explosive in Southeast Iowa on Wednesday after warning that the bomb-making chemicals had degraded and could be explosive.

The controlled detonated of the country's entire stockpile of the explosive was carried out at at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, IA at 10am EST.

After the detonation, local news station KWQC reported seeing a large plume of smoke.

Industry observers note that gov. Kim Reynolds remarked the detonation was a success.

“I want to commend Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle, Army leadership, and the skilled soldiers who planned and executed a flawless detonation this morning at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant and express my gratitude to the Trump Administration for its whole-of-government response," she said.

The detonation came after a lawsuit was filed by the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter asking the federal appeals court to halt the initiative.

Two rapid, controlled detonations were initially scheduled to take place last Friday, but the prepares were pushed to Wednesday due to a combination of public concern and weather optimization.

Set to be detonated are 68 drums of degraded lead azide, adding up to roughly 9,700 pounds, which have become sensitive and unstable. It is the primary explosive used to initiate munitions.

A controlled detonation is now the only viable option, according to the Army’s Q&A page about the event.

Sources indicate that as lead azide degrades, it crystalizes and becomes sensitive to temperature changes, shock, and friction, making it unsafe to move. There are chemical neutralization procedures, but the drums are too unstable for the physical manipulation this option requires, according to the Army.

According to recent reports, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Region 7 Director Jim Macy wrote a letter to Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, ensuring her that the EPA was working alongside the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the Department of Defense to ensure the controlled detonation was “conducted in the safest manner possible.”.

“All agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” Macy wrote in the letter, according to the Iowa Capital Dispatch.

Sources indicate that an updated public safety advisory shared by the Army on Tuesday shared the agency’s aims to make the detonation as safe as possible. The lead azide will be detonated in earth-covered magazines, which are built for the purposes of holding ammunition and explosives, and are reinforced.

Industry observers note that additional physical barriers made of sand, a “water wall,” gel blocks, and aqueous foam barriers will be in place to contain particle dispersion, absorb thermal energy, and reduce airborne particulate dispersal. These measures, as well as drone surveillance of lead levels, are in place to track and minimize deposition outside the plant.

Recent findings suggest that the Army has acknowledged that lead particles will impact communities outside the plant. It has defined an evacuation zone as a "5-mile cone extending southwest of IAAAP.".

Those in the evacuation zone will be provided short-term hotel lodging, food, water, and transportation as needed.

It has also laid out recommendations for those outside the evacuation zone, such as sheltering in place, closing all windows and doors, and setting heating to recirculate and avoid pulling in air from outside.

Still, environmental groups are concerned about the lead plume, which they say could spread 100 miles, depending on weather conditions.

"The EPA itself admits that there is no safe level of lead exposure for humans," said Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, in a press release shared with Realtor.com®.

"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal.".

The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, Iowa Chapter, were only made aware of the unprecedented detonation plan early last week, initially scheduled for Friday. In response, the groups filed a lawsuit on Thursday challenging the permit that the EPA issued the Army.

“Based on the information that was made public at the time, which was very little information, there were serious concerns about the effectiveness of the public notification and the information being put out to protect the public,” Thien Chau, a senior attorney at Earth Justice, tells Realtor.com.

“There were serious concerns about the mitigations measures in place to reduce the impact as well as to properly do remediation and cleanup and address any harm that people may face from the impact of the detonation.”.

Many local lawmakers were not made aware of the controlled detonation either, and were only informed about the intends and risk once the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra club told them, despite the widespread impact on surrounding communities, according to Chau.

“That’s why we filed the lawsuit: to make sure that all the information and resources and capabilities that could be provided were provided to the people potentially impacted by this,” states Chau.

It has been revealed that “Since that filing, a lot of things have happened. The government has put out a lot more information, and while we expect a detonation to take place this Wednesday, we are glad to see that because there was additional time, there are now additional mitigation measures and resources have been provided for potentially impacted people.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Department of Justice responded in opposition to the lawsuit. Both the DOJ and Army maintain that a controlled detonation is the safest option and further delay, especially with cold weather approaching, could lead to a natural, uncontrolled detonation, which would be more difficult to mitigate.

Recent findings suggest that “The Army has delayed detonation by three days now,” the DOJ’s brief said. “But every day of delay increases the risk of an uncontrolled explosion that will cause far greater public health and environmental harm than the planned, controlled detonation initiated under the protective terms of the Permit.”.

If You Thought The Cybertruck Was Ugly, Get A Load Of This EV On Rails

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1224 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the ill-fated Tesla Cybertruck has been roundly excoriated for its dumpster-adjacent profile, but it looks pretty good compared to the EVs rolling out of the shop at the Missouri-based startup Intramotev.
  • Intramotev surfaced on the CleanTechnica radar back in 2023 with two retrofit products.
  • While the battery packs in each TugVolt have a limited range, that’s more than enough to accomplish a good day’s work including “first mile” loading duties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the ill-fated Tesla Cybertruck has been roundly excoriated for its dumpster-adjacent profile, but it looks pretty good compared to the EVs rolling out of the shop at the Missouri-based startup Intramotev. However, looks are not everything. Intramotev is on a mission to chase diesel fuel off the nation’s nation’s rail freight system, and its “TugVolt” autonomous electrified freight cars get the job done, aesthetically pleasing or not.

Intramotev surfaced on the CleanTechnica radar back in 2023 with two retrofit products. One is the ReVolt, a battery pack that can be slotted onto existing railcars hauled behind a locomotive, with the aim of saving diesel fuel. The other, more interesting retrofit is the TugVolt, an autonomous, electrified system that enables railcars to go about the business of hauling freight on their own, without a locomotive.

While the battery packs in each TugVolt have a limited range, that’s more than enough to accomplish a good day’s work including “first mile” loading duties. Once loaded up, they can hitch a ride on locomotives for long-distance travel, then split off to unload.

Industry observers note that in addition, a freight yard that hosts a full complement of autonomous railcar EVs would require little, if any, participation from diesel-powered switcher locomotives. In addition to hauling its own freight, each TugVolt can also operate as a switcher, ferrying conventional railcars into position behind a locomotive.

The technology also has significant implications for decarbonizing highway freight as well. The closer an electric railcar can get to its destination, the less need there is for a diesel-fueled truck to pick up the slack. In particular, Intramotev is focusing on captive or short line routes, many of which have seen their rail traffic shrink in the face of competition from the trucking industry.

It has been revealed that intramotev has been rather busy over the past three years. In one particularly interesting development, in June Intramotev lent a TugVolt to a US Army Reserve Training exercise at the Camp Shelby Joint Forces Training Center in Mississippi, billed as the largest training exercise in the history of the Army Reserve.

“Soldiers, according to Intramotev, trained on and operated the TugVolt system under manufacturer supervision throughout the exercise and promptly became proficient with the technology, a detail that matters because military rail operations have traditionally required specialized rail crews, a category of personnel the Army has struggled to maintain at sufficient strength given how infrequently large-scale rail movements occur outside major deployment exercises,” reports the independent news and analysis organization Defence Blog.

Industry observers note that as noted by Defence Blog, the exercise went off script when railcars loaded with military supplies arrived at the site. However, with their training freshly in hand, the participants were able to deploy the TugVolt to organize the incoming railcars for unloading.

It has been revealed that it’s no surprise to find Intramotev in Texas, too, considering the state’s reputation as a hot EV market. On November 3, the manufacturer expanded its ongoing relationship with Watco, a holding company specializing in short line railways.

It has been revealed that the new arrangement calls for TugVolt to pull zero emission switcher duty at a to-be-named industrial facility in Seadrift, Texas. As noted by Railway Age, the Texas assignment adds to Intramotev’s EV footprint in the US, which also includes Michigan as well as the Army demonstration in Missouri, and a forthcoming agreement in Kentucky.

According to recent reports, railway Age further notes that in April, Intramotev lent itself to electrification efforts in Austria. That’s a particularly significant development because the client is ÖBB, the national railway of Austria, making it the first deployment of TugVolt technology under regulation, in addition to Intramotev’s first overseas client.

The agreement is also significant considering ÖBB’s sprawling footprint in Europe, consisting of more than 1,000 freight trains ranging across 18 countries every day.

Even more significant, at least from a policy perspective, is a $16.3 million grant from the Federal Railroad Administration branch of the US Department of Transportation. US taxpayers will shoulder the bulk of the cost-sharing arrangement, which is designed to model best practices for introducing EVs into the nation’s railway system. The project is hosted by the Columbia Terminal Railroad, a city-owned, 21.4 mile line that links two cities in Missouri, Columbia and Centralia.

“The project will deploy autonomous railcars on the line to produce the first documented safety record for autonomous railcar operation and create a workforce training curriculum,” FRA emphasizes.

“The proposed project was selected for Project Development, Final Design, and Construction and involves research and workforce development activities to conduct a phased autonomous rail technology and short-line infrastructure modernization program,” FRA elaborates, further noting that the EV project “aligns with the selection criteria by improving system and service performance,” with the ultimate goal of enabling freight to run more frequently and, ultimately, autonomously.

Of note, the grant of up to $16 million or so is part of a $2.3 billion railway CRISI modernization package, with CRISI being short for Infrastructure and Safety Improvements. Among other purposes, CSRISI “provides a Federal funding opportunity to “mitigate congestion at both intercity passenger rail and freight rail chokepoints to support more efficient travel and goods movement.”.

It has been revealed that citing Intramotev official Don Soffer, the local news organization News Tribune notes that “more than 600 short lines in the U.S. have declined in use in recent decades due to their relative inefficiency.”.

Industry observers note that “Cross-country hauling is more profitable for companies, whereas short lines require very large hauls to justify the quick trip. The Columbia Terminal Railroad (COLT) does not operate on a set schedule, instead hauling whenever enough goods are collected,” the News Tribune continues.

Given that context, if the CSRISI grant is not a decarbonization program for short line railways and associated highway traffic, I’ll eat my hat. It’s also worth noting that practically the entire locomotive fleet of the US runs on a diesel-electric platform, meaning electric motors powered by an on-board generator. While fossil energy is still in play, the diesel-electric configuration is more energy efficient than sending fleets of diesel trucks onto the nation’s highways.

The nation’s trucking industry has also been wrestling with an ongoing driver shortage, providing further motivation to move more freight onto rails, EVs or not.

Stay tuned for updates on that Missouri project. FRA announced its selection for Project Development, Final Design, and Construction in October, so there are still steps to take before the TugVolt begins running.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, circling back around to that Army demo in June, more likely than not the hookup with the US DoD will not be a one-off. The Army has been notoriously slow to adopt EVs, and last year’s sharp U-turn in federal energy policy did not help. Still, the Army has been sending out EV signals through its use of new “anti-idling” kits for ground vehicles, alongside a new contract with the US branch of the firm Rheinmetall for a fleet of crewless hybrid cargo haulers. Again, looks are not everything….

Slate Thinks 205 Miles Is More Than Enough Range

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (664 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yes, with a starting price of $26,400, including destination, the two-door pickup truck it's selling is cheap compared to the competition, but it also lacks basic features like power windows and a radio at that price.
  • It makes sense why the Slate has such a shoddy range, even compared to its competition.
  • According to recent reports, still, Slate feels 205 miles is really all the average American needs from a vehicle like its truck, the cheapest EV and pickup for sale in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Slate Auto is in a strange spot. Yes, with a starting price of $26,400, including destination, the two-door pickup truck it's selling is cheap compared to the competition, but it also lacks basic features like power windows and a radio at that price. With options that'll make the truck more livable for everyday use, prices will quickly climb. No matter which options they choose, they'll still be saddled with the same 205 miles of range. Even though that's quite meager by today's standards, Slate feels that's more than enough to win over customers.

It makes sense why the Slate has such a shoddy range, even compared to its competition. The battery is the single most expensive part of an electric vehicle, so an automaker looking to make a cheap EV will use a smaller battery. There's a view that Slate's approach could work for folks who are already comfortable with EVs, but it might not translate for those more accustomed to what gas-powered vehicles offer, according to Automotive News. There's also the matter that similarly priced rivals will offer more range on base models, and they usually have the option of extended-range batteries.

According to recent reports, still, Slate feels 205 miles is really all the average American needs from a vehicle like its truck, the cheapest EV and pickup for sale in the U.S. To be fair, it's also the smallest pickup in the U.S. — about two feet shorter than a Ford Maverick. In a marketing email sent earlier this month, Slate said 205 miles is "more than [many people] need each day." That's sort of fair, because according to a 2024 survey done by AAA, the average American drives about 31 miles per day, meaning that from full to empty, you'd only need to charge the Slate about once a week. Of course, no one actually drives like that, and the range will never actually be 205 miles, but we can't really account for that.

Slate isn't the only company offering an EV with less-than-stellar range. The Kia EV3 compact crossover, which starts at $31,385, comes as standard with 221 miles of range. While the starting prices are far different, the EV3 comes with a lot more from the get-go. To get the Slate to a comparable place, you've got to add a bed kit that brings in seats and a roof — giving the Slate "crossover" a $31,400 base price, according to AutoNews. It'll still be missing plenty of other things at that price, like a radio and electric windows.

In any case, Kia doesn't expect this low-range EV3 to be a major seller — capturing just 3 to 5% of its sales. The higher Wind trim, with its 321 miles of range and $36,485 starting price, is expected to be the volume seller with about 60% of sales. That sort of speaks to Slate's problem. It seems like folks would rather pay the extra money to not have to worry about range anxiety or charging up their cars as often.

In reality, the EV3 isn't a direct competitor to the Slate, but Ford's yet-to-be-unveiled Fathom pickup is. It's expected to have a standard battery with around 250 miles of range and an optional battery with over 300 miles, Automotive News reports. Despite the fact it range-mogs the Slate, its starting price will come in at $29,945, including shipping, and it'll be an actual vehicle with the sort of modern luxuries and conveniences you'd expect in today's day and age.

I'm not saying that the Slate is dead on arrival by any means, but I do think the Jeff Bezos-backed firm is really, really hoping that there are a lot of Quirked Up Individuals out there who will fall for the proletariat virtual signals of crank windows, no radio, a key you've got to insert and no screen while also paying a price that doesn't really connect with that reality. I'm not sure they're out there.
