📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Industry Voices—The case for social prescribing in older adult care" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Loneliness and social isolation often show up in the exam room through an older patient’s high blood pressure, worsening depression or recent emergency department visit.

Lack of social connection is an increasingly common risk factor for both physical and mental health conditions that clinicians often recognize—but may not feel well-equipped to treat.

Approximately one in four older Americans is socially isolated, and more than four in 10 report feeling lonely. Both are associated with high rates of morbidity and mortality, including elevated risks of heart disease, stroke, cognitive decline and dementia. Social isolation is also associated with an additional $6.7 billion in Medicare spending, mainly from avoidable hospital and nursing home utilization.

It has been revealed that as leaders of foundations committed to improving the health and well-being of older adults, we invest heavily in programs that foster social connection, especially for underserved populations. But to truly address this public health epidemic, healthcare providers must be part of the solution.

Industry observers note that clinicians can play an essential role in identifying lonely and isolated patients and referring them to resources that promote social engagement. Integrating social prescribing into clinical workflows presents challenges in the current U.S. payment system, but promising approaches are showing success and can be replicated.

Sources indicate that food as Medicine (FAM) programs have already expanded our understanding of what a prescription can encompass. While physicians regularly recommend that patients adopt a healthy diet, that advice is rarely heeded for both behavioral and socioeconomic reasons. What has made a difference is a clinician’s prescribing of free or affordable individualized interventions in partnership with community-based resources and with systemwide support.

Similarly, social prescribing is a structured, team-based intervention that involves assessing and addressing loneliness and social isolation as part of a patient’s care plan. Taking the patient’s individualized needs and circumstances into account, a referral is made to a community organization or program that fosters social connections. These activities can range from in-person group programs to virtual activities or telephone-based companionship for people with mobility or transportation barriers.

In the United Kingdom (U.K.), Canada and Australia, established social prescribing programs have been linked to reductions in emergency department visits, hospitalizations and healthcare spending.

According to recent reports, brief, validated assessment tools, such as the UCLA-3-Item Loneliness Scale and the condensed Berkman-Syme Social Network Index, can be incorporated into the routine patient health questionnaires to help identify those at risk. Hospitals have a new incentive to use these screens with the recently implemented Age-Friendly Hospital Measure from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which includes addressing social vulnerability as one of five required domains.

Recent findings suggest that but what then? Identifying suitable programs, partnering with local organizations, and making those connections for patients is a job in itself, one that clinicians cannot reasonably be expected to add to their already full workload. And this is especially complicated in rural areas where both clinicians and programs are more likely to be limited.

In a recent development, in the U.K., they have designated “link workers” to fill this role. Here in the U.S., value-based care team practices, which are becoming more common, can support a similar position or share those responsibilities among team members. A Social Prescribing Learning Hub from Social Prescribing USA offers practical guidance for how providers can get started, including choosing community partners and models, measuring impact and navigating the insurance landscape.

The state of Connecticut has taken a different approach by building a social prescribing infrastructure in collaboration with SocialRx, a organization that matches patients with appropriate programs, enabling healthcare providers to prescribe participation in arts and cultural activities that are free to state residents. Other states, including Georgia, Massachusetts and California, have developed similar social prescribing ecosystems.

It has been revealed that some insurers and care providers are creating their own social connection programs. BCBS of Massachusetts has partnered with Elder Services of Worcester Area to reduce emergency department utilization among their Medicare Advantage members by providing Transition Coaches after hospitalizations or ED visits. The coaches screen patients for isolation and loneliness, connect them with social groups and companion visits, and help them use technology to stay connected with family, friends and healthcare providers.

Building a sustainable social prescribing infrastructure also requires government and philanthropic support for evidence-based programs that foster social connections in spaces where older adults commonly gather. One example is the American Library Association’s Aging Together initiative, supported by The John A. Hartford Foundation, which strengthens public library programs that reduce social isolation and promote older adults' health and well-being.

Other countries’ experience with social prescribing is building evidence of its effectiveness in improving social connectedness and health outcomes, as shown in a recently released evidence roundup from the Center for Health Care Strategies. However, more research is needed on how to implement effective social prescribing practices in the U.S. One such effort is a partnership between the Humana Foundation and the Aspen Institute to evaluate the prescribing, dosage and follow-up of relationship-building volunteer activities for diverse, underserved older adults who screen for loneliness or social isolation.

Industry observers note that there is growing recognition of loneliness and social isolation as clinical risk factors impacting older adults’ health, independence and quality of life. Health professionals can play an essential role in identifying these risk factors and making social engagement a part of patients’ care prepares. Support from health systems, philanthropy and the government is needed to staff and train teams, identify effective engagement strategies, build community partnerships, and establish pathways for referrals and follow-up. Working together, healthcare and community organizations can make social prescribing a practical component of age-friendly, whole-person care.

Tiffany Benjamin is CEO of the Humana Foundation. Rani E. Snyder is President of The John A. Hartford Foundation.

In a recent development, editor's note: The Humana Foundation provides support to The Aspen Institute. The John A. Hartford Foundation provides support to the American Library Association Aging Together initiative, the Social Prescribing USA Learning Hub, and the Center for Health Care Strategies' evidence roundup.

Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that vitamin C may do more than support everyday health.
  • Exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades.
  • It has been revealed that one of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that vitamin C may do more than support everyday health. Upcoming research from the University of Waterloo suggests that it could also help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming during digestion. Using mathematical modeling, scientists investigated how vitamin C influences chemical reactions in the digestive system that have been linked to cancer risk.

Exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades. These compounds are found in cured meats such as bacon and salami, as well as in fruits and vegetables grown in soil or water affected by pollution. Although nitrates and nitrites contribute to important functions in the brain and cardiovascular system, they can also participate in potentially harmful reactions once they reach the stomach.

It has been revealed that one of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development. Understanding what causes these chemicals to form, and what might prevent their formation, has been a longstanding challenge.

Why Vitamin C Could Change the Cancer Risk Equation.

"Since at least the 90s, researchers have been studying the link between cancer and these compounds, with conflicting results," remarked Dr. Gordon McNicol, a post-doctoral researcher in applied mathematics and the first author of the study. "Our work suggests that the presence of dietary Vitamin C may help explain these inconsistencies.".

To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body and undergo chemical changes. The model incorporated several interconnected systems, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma, the liquid portion of blood.

It has been revealed that their simulations revealed that vitamin C consumed alongside nitrates and nitrites may interfere with the formation of potentially harmful compounds. This could help explain why foods containing nitrates do not necessarily carry the same risks.

Recent findings suggest that for example, leafy vegetables such as spinach naturally contain both nitrates and vitamin C. According to the model, the presence of vitamin C could limit the chemical reactions associated with cancer risk, potentially helping explain the protective effects suggested by some dietary research.

Could Taking Vitamin C After Meals Help?

The researchers also explored whether vitamin C supplements might offer similar benefits when taken after eating.

Their findings suggest that taking vitamin C after each meal could moderately reduce the formation of nitrosation products associated with cancer risk. This effect could be particularly relevant when consuming foods containing nitrates and nitrites, including processed meats such as bacon and salami.

Recent findings suggest that however, the results come from mathematical simulations rather than clinical trials. Although the model predicts that vitamin C can reduce the production of potentially harmful chemicals, further research is needed to determine whether this translates into a measurable reduction in cancer risk in humans.

New Clues for Future Cancer Prevention Research.

It has been revealed that the researchers believe their model could help scientists better understand the complicated relationship between diet, digestive chemistry, and cancer risk. It may also provide guidance for future experiments examining how nutritional choices influence the formation of potentially harmful compounds.

It has been revealed that "This work provides a mechanistic roadmap for future clinical and laboratory studies by identifying the key interacting drivers of these potentially harmful chemical reactions, including nitrite exposure, antioxidant intake, meal timing, gastric conditions and oral microbiome activity," said Dr. Anita Layton, professor of applied mathematics and Canada 150 researcher chair. "This model can help researchers design more targeted experiments and interventions, focusing on when and in whom nitrosation is most likely to occur.".

By identifying how factors such as vitamin C intake, meal timing, stomach conditions, and bacteria in the mouth interact, the model could help researchers develop more precise strategies for studying and potentially reducing cancer-related chemical reactions during digestion.

The study, "Vitamin C as a nitrosation inhibitor: A modelling study across dietary patterns and water quality," was published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.

Thanksgiving Nor’easter Postpones Macy’s Parade and Targets Over 250 Million: The Latest on Power Outages, Homes at Risk, and More

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A nor'easter and even a "bomb cyclone" are predicted to slam the Northeast on Thanksgiving this year, putting millions in a path of destruction not seen on the holiday for decades—and causing a time honored tradition to be postponed for the first time in its history.
  • Heavy rain, high winds, and coastal impacts to the East Coast are remarked to begin on Wednesday and carry through Thanksgiving, according to NOAA's Weather Prediction Center.
  • The biggest impact will be seen starting in the Southeast, before moving its way to the Northeast, Great Lakes, and Ohio Valley.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A nor'easter and even a "bomb cyclone" are predicted to slam the Northeast on Thanksgiving this year, putting millions in a path of destruction not seen on the holiday for decades—and causing a time honored tradition to be postponed for the first time in its history.

Heavy rain, high winds, and coastal impacts to the East Coast are remarked to begin on Wednesday and carry through Thanksgiving, according to NOAA's Weather Prediction Center.

The biggest impact will be seen starting in the Southeast, before moving its way to the Northeast, Great Lakes, and Ohio Valley.

While flooding is a major consideration, meteorologists are more concerned about the powerful winds accompanying the storm, which could result in tree damage, power outages, and other disasters for homeowners to contend with on the significant day.

The high winds ultimately forced the hands of Newly introduced York City officials, the NYPD and Macy's, who late on Wednesday declared that the parade would be pushed off until the following Saturday Nov. 28, due to the weather.

The storm will ramp up in the Southeast on Wednesday, according to The Weather Channel, with rain, wind, and coastal flooding causing hazardous conditions for travelers heading home for the holiday.

Because temperatures have dropped as well, snow is also likely in parts of Missouri and Illinois beginning later in the day, continuing into the night, into Thanksgiving.

By Thanksgiving Thursday, the storm will have made its way north into the mid-Atlantic and Ohio Valley, before steadily moving into Latest England by afternoon or evening.

While wind is top of mind given the milestone parade, significant coastal flooding along the East Coast is poised to cause beach erosion, flooded coastal streets, and potential structural damage.

Moderate to major flooding is possible from Georgia to Long Island, alongside at least minor flooding in Newly introduced England, with any heavy rain during high tide worsening the inundation, says Weather.com.

Peak water levels will hit Georgia and South Carolina on Wednesday morning, before shifting north to North Carolina, Virginia, Delaware, the Jersey Shore, and Long Island on Thanksgiving morning, and reaching coastal Upcoming England by Thursday and Friday midday.

Conditions could be especially severe in the mid-Atlantic, with widespread road flooding expected across Jersey Shore communities such as Atlantic City and Ocean City, water levels in Cape May and coastal Delaware potentially hitting their highest mark since January 2016, and Ocean City, MD, approaching its 1998 all-time record.

As the storm threatened to ground the balloons and drench the anticipated thousands of spectators, local outlets reported early Wednesday that Mayor Mamdani, the police commissioner and Macy's executives will announce the postponement of the Thanksgiving parade late on Wednesday.

The parade was scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. EST on Thursday, on Manhattan’s Upper West Side, and the National Weather Service had already issued a high wind warning before the call was made to move the parade.

The last reports predict that wind gusts will already exceed limits before the parade is even set to start.

"There is a significant risk that gusty winds ahead of the nor’easter cause the parade balloons to at least be lower than usual, and it’s possible they are not able to fly at all," AccuWeather Vice President of Forecast Operations Dan DePodwin said ahead of the announcement .

Industry observers note that "This scenario is most likely should the storm move a bit more swiftly up the coast. If it’s slower, the wind may intensify after the parade is over.".

Sustained winds must remain below 23 mph and gusts have to be lower than 34 mph for the balloons to fly.

The last balloon grounding was in 1971, but the parade has never been canceled due to weather in its 100-year history.

Power outages and tree damage are possible, according to the Weather Prediction Center, as wind gusts of 50-plus mph are forecasted along the coast with 40-plus mph gusts inland into the Interstate-95 corridor through at least Friday.

As of Monday evening, the National Weather Service warned that “tree damage and power outages will be possible” from the storm on Thanksgiving Day.

The forecasts put the strongest gusts along the mid-Atlantic coast and inland corridors on Thursday. Along the Upcoming Jersey shore and Delaware beaches, gusts will reach 50 to 60 mph—with 40 to 50 mph inland—prompting NWS Mount Holly to concern a high wind watch for the coastal strip from late Wednesday night through late Thursday night.

Farther south, Southeast Virginia and Northeast North Carolina face 2 to 3 inches of rain alongside east to northeast gusts of 40 to 50 mph inland and potentially 50 to 60 mph on the coast, where NWS Wakefield noted a high wind watch may be needed. Meanwhile, Washington, DC, Baltimore, and Northern Virginia can expect 1 to 3 inches of rain and Thanksgiving Day gusts of 35 to 50 mph, which NWS Sterling warned could be “strong to perhaps damaging.”.

The threat shifts northward later in the day, with Southern New England forecast to see gusts of 40 to 55 mph and up to 60 mph on Cape Cod and the islands. According to NWS Boston, the strongest winds in that region will arrive on Thursday night. In Rhode Island, forecasters specifically note the potential for isolated power outages late Thursday night and overnight, with coastal areas facing the highest risk.

Meanwhile, California has its own winter weather whirlwind to contend with, including massive waves battering the coastline.

According to the NWS, record-breaking king tides, combined with elevated surf and a large Pacific swell, are expected to bring significant coastal flooding to Southern California during this Thanksgiving week, with the greatest impacts anticipated Wednesday and Thursday, potentially flooding coastal properties and causing significant beach erosion.

“A series of winter storms is impacting California, bringing heavy rain, mountain snow, and potentially hazardous travel conditions,” the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services stated on Friday.

The mayor of San Francisco warned of “high tides and rain that this city has never seen before,” in the days leading up to the holiday, asking the public to avoid all but essential travel. The National Weather Service in the Bay Area added low areas would be prone to flooding, including San Francisco International Airport, which would be an added hindrance to travel to say the least.

Meanwhile, Southern California cities such as Newport Beach, Seal Beach, and Long Beach have put up miles of sand berms, some 15 feet tall or higher, to try to keep the ocean back, according to The Washington Post.

This weather seems to be a perfect storm of the warm waters of record-breaking El Niño colliding with an extra-high “king tide,” which the area already had to contend with a few weeks ago.

"In California, tides will be about half a foot higher than the highest in October," physical oceanographer Greg Dusek told Weather.com.

"This means that even if El Niño doesn't increase water levels further, there will be significant flooding along the California coast," Dusek noted.

Forecasts predict the worst of the storms could strike on Tuesday and Wednesday night into Thanksgiving Day.

MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that while we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful.
  • Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain.
  • The finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful. Sleep provides an crucial opportunity to clear away these substances. As we rest, waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) move through the brain, helping remove waste and maintain healthy brain function.

Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain. Those stronger electrical signals, in turn, produce larger waves of CSF.

The finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health. Scientists want to determine whether increasing this fluid movement could sharpen thinking, strengthen memory, or slow neurodegenerative diseases associated with the accumulation of damaging proteins, including amyloid beta.

Sources indicate that "We found that we were able to increase the size of the CSF flow wave during sleep, which as far as we know, there hasn't been a method to do before. Now that we can enhance CSF flow during sleep in healthy adults, we're really excited to bring this technology to clinical populations to see what effects we can have," says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Recent findings suggest that lewis led the research as senior author. The findings were published in Science Translational Medicine, with Joshua Levitt serving as lead author. Levitt recently completed his PhD at Boston University and previously worked as a visiting graduate student in Lewis' laboratory.

How Sleep Helps the Brain Remove Waste.

In a recent development, cerebrospinal fluid is a transparent liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, providing protection against physical injury. It also supports brain function by transporting nutrients, including glucose, and carrying away waste released by brain cells as they consume energy.

In 2019, Lewis demonstrated that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) could be used to observe the movement of CSF into and out of the brain during sleep. Her team found that this movement closely follows slow electrical brain waves, which are especially prominent during deep sleep.

In a recent development, building on that discovery, the researchers wanted to understand whether deliberately strengthening these electrical waves would also increase the movement of CSF. Earlier experiments had shown that sounds presented at precisely the right moment could enhance slow brain waves.

Recent findings suggest that "You can make more of these electrical slow waves through an auditory stimulus, if it comes at just the right time. Similar to a child on a swing, if you push them when they're at the right moment in their movement, you can make that swing go farther," Lewis says. "The challenge is: How do you find just the right time?".

How Pink Noise Amplifies Brain Waves.

It has been revealed that to test the idea, the team used extremely short bursts of pink noise, each lasting just 50 milliseconds. Pink noise contains the full range of frequencies that humans can hear, much like white noise. However, its lower frequencies are more prominent, while higher frequencies are quieter. The result is a softer, more balanced sound reminiscent of steady rainfall or a waterfall heard from a distance.

Timing was essential. The researchers needed to deliver each burst of sound when a sleeping participant's slow brain waves reached their peak. To identify those moments, they monitored electrical activity using EEG while simultaneously measuring CSF movement with fMRI.

According to recent reports, combining the two measurements created a technical obstacle. The powerful magnetic fields used in fMRI interfere with EEG recordings, making it difficult to detect the brain's electrical signals accurately and swiftly enough to synchronize the sound.

The team addressed this problem by creating a method that removes interference from EEG signals in less than 100 milliseconds. They also designed an algorithm capable of predicting when the next slow wave peak would occur, compensating for the small delay introduced by processing the signals. Together, these advances made it possible to play each burst of pink noise at the intended moment.

Stronger Brain Cleaning Waves During Sleep.

According to recent reports, the researchers tested their approach in 14 healthy volunteers. They found that the carefully timed sounds increased the size of both the brain's slow electrical waves and the accompanying CSF waves. Importantly, the sounds were quiet enough that they did not wake the participants.

The brain scans also helped explain how the process works. Slow electrical waves were associated with blood vessels narrowing and widening, creating a pumping effect that pushes CSF out of the brain. These slow waves occur during non-REM sleep and become increasingly pronounced as sleep deepens.

By enhancing the electrical waves, the researchers were able to strengthen the fluid movement associated with the brain's natural waste removal process. However, the study did not directly establish whether the stronger CSF waves actually removed more waste or improved sleep quality.

Could Pink Noise Improve Sleep and Help Fight Alzheimer's?

The researchers now want to investigate whether increasing CSF flow leads to more refreshing, restorative sleep, particularly for people who struggle with insomnia. Another major goal is to determine whether the technique can improve the brain's ability to clear harmful substances.

This possibility is especially relevant to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, which are associated with the accumulation of abnormal proteins in the brain. If stronger CSF movement ultimately translates into more effective waste removal, the approach could offer a new way to address one of the biological processes involved in these conditions.

It has been revealed that "Brain waste clearance is really important for Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia, which are caused, in part, by the buildup of molecules like amyloid and tau in the brain. If we can improve brain waste clearance, we may be able to help prevent the buildups of these plaques that lead to disease," Levitt notes.

According to recent reports, the technology could eventually become accessible outside research laboratories. Levitt has launched a company that aims to develop a home device, potentially in the form of a headband, that would deliver sound at the appropriate moments during sleep to increase CSF flow.

For now, the results demonstrate that a simple auditory stimulus, when precisely synchronized with brain activity, can alter the fluid waves associated with the brain's nighttime cleaning process. Whether those changes can translate into better sleep, stronger memory, or protection against neurodegenerative disease remains an notable question for future studies.

The research received funding from a McKnight Scholar Award, a Sloan Fellowship, a Pew Biomedical Scholars Award, the Simons Foundation Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, the MIT EECS Transformative Research Fund, the National Institutes of Health, the Corundum Convergence Institute, and the Panasonic Well Fellowship for AI and Wellness.

Epochal launches with $100M to help developers train predictive AI models

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that artificial intelligence tooling startup Epochal AI Inc.
  • The capital was provided by Chief Executive Officer Guodong Zhang, a machine learning researcher who earlier co-founded xAI Corp.
  • Epochal’s first offering is a cloud service called the Epochal Time Portal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:30 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

It has been revealed that artificial intelligence tooling startup Epochal AI Inc. launched today with $100 million in funding.

The capital was provided by Chief Executive Officer Guodong Zhang, a machine learning researcher who earlier co-founded xAI Corp. He established Epochal earlier this year with two other xAI co-founders, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss. The company’s staff also includes former researchers from Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC and Google DeepMind.

Epochal’s first offering is a cloud service called the Epochal Time Portal. According to the manufacturer, it enables developers to train AI models that can predict future events. The service does so by providing models with access to historical web data from the past 30 years.

If a bank wishes to train an AI that can predict quarterly earnings, it could use the service to fetch financial results from the first three quarters of 2025. It could then ask the AI to estimate fourth-quarter results from the same year.

Sources indicate that after the model generates its predictions, developers can compare them against real fourth-quarter earnings to check the model’s accuracy. They can make adjustments if necessary and then repeat the training workflow until the model starts generating accurate forecasts.

The Epochal Time Portal features more than 1 trillion historical web pages on launch. Each entry includes a timestamp that indicates when it was created. According to the manufacturer, its timestamps make it possible to track how a web page changed over time.

In a recent development, AI models access the content through a purpose-built search engine. It enables them to specify the time periods from which they wish to retrieve web pages. According to Epochal, its platform provides one-minute granularity for the most frequently updated pages.

It has been revealed that like consumer search engines, the Epochal Time Portal prioritizes the web pages that are most relevant to each given query. The difference is that it considers web pages’ creation date when evaluating relevance. If a query contains the term “Meta” but asks for pages created before 2021, the year Facebook Inc. rebranded, the Epochal Time Portal will not bring up pages that relate to the social networking giant.

Recent findings suggest that today’s frontier models can determine that they’re being trained on historical data rather than up-to-date information. For example, a model might compare the creation date of a web page to the virtual clock of the operating system on which it deployed. Such discrepancies can lower the effectiveness of training runs.

Recent findings suggest that according to Epochal, its service mitigates the glitch by deploying AI models in sandboxes synced to their training data. If a manufacturer is training a model on we pages from 2025, the Epochal Time Portal will run it on a Linux version from that year. It applies the same precautions to the software tools and programming language versions that models use.

Industry observers note that the Epochal Time Portal is initially available in a single free tier with low usage limits. Epochal plans to follow up the launch by sharing the results of several AI experiments that its researchers have carried out using the service.

Tech Report: How messaging could be the next source of clinician burnout

How messaging could be the next source of clinician burnout" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Physician burnout may be falling nationally, but healthcare leaders are noting a potential new source of overwhelm: messaging overload.

And, it’s not affecting all providers equally.

Leaders at Ochsner Health, per the American Medical Association (AMA), found female physicians receive about 30% more staff messages and 30% more patient messages than their male counterparts through an analysis of electronic health record (EHR) data.

Though the direct causes are unknown, TigerConnect Chief Growth Officer Sheeza Hussain said general messaging overload is a “symptom of a coordination problem.”.

“Healthcare slows down when people are waiting for information, decisions, consults, transfers, and discharges and all the handoffs in between,” Hussain noted. “At TigerConnect, we focus on helping health systems remove those bottlenecks by connecting people, systems and workflows so communication moves care forward.”.

Hussain continued, “When communication is orchestrated well, clinicians can focus on care, and patients can move through their care journey more smoothly and effectively.”.

Hussain and Nikki Manuel, TigerConnect clinical solution design director, spoke with Fierce Healthcare about the factors driving this trend, impacts on patient experience and how health systems can mitigate it.

Editor’s note: The following Q&A has been edited for length and clarity.

Fierce Healthcare: Why does message overload land unevenly in hospitals and health systems?

In a recent development, nikki Manuel: Nurses are at the center of patient care and care coordination, so a significant share of the communication burden often falls on them. Think about a nurse trying to reach the right provider about a change in a patient’s condition. They may need to review the EHR, confirm who is on call, determine the preferred communication method and follow up if there is no response—all while managing other patients. The burden grows when communication crosses departments or shifts and ownership is unclear. The clinicians coordinating those handoffs can end up spending valuable time navigating the communication process instead of moving more quickly to the next step in care.

Sheeza Hussain: In my conversations with health system leaders, it comes back to fragmentation. Healthcare has never lacked technology, but more technology hasn’t created more connected care. Hospitals run single-purpose communication tools, fleets of devices, and disconnected biomedical equipment, putting out huge volumes of alerts and alarms. None of it coordinates, which puts clinicians in the role of middleware. It’s not a tool shortage. It’s a coordination problem.

FH: As this trend takes shape, who are the clinicians most affected by potential overload?

Hussain: Nurses, first. They’re asked to manually bridge disconnected systems and respond to alarms. Most alarms don’t need a response, but a nurse still has to hear every one to find out. Hospitalists and on-call physicians feel it too, especially when coverage isn’t clear. Clinicians should not be middleware.

FH: How, if at all, is messaging overload shaping up to be the next source of burnout for clinicians?

Industry observers note that manuel: I don’t think messaging itself is necessarily the next source of burnout. In many ways, messaging has made communication easier. As a bedside nurse, I remember relying on pagers and phone calls and having to stop what I was doing when a provider called back. Messaging gives clinicians more flexibility to communicate without constantly interrupting patient care.

The burden comes when we layer messaging onto communication processes that haven’t been standardized. Nurses are already surrounded by alerts, messages, and notifications coming from multiple systems, and they’re often the ones deciding what needs action, who needs to receive it, and what to do when there isn’t a response. That’s where the cognitive load starts to build.

Health systems should be looking at where communication can be standardized and where alerts, routing and escalation can be automated. Technology should support that process by identifying the appropriate person and helping get the right information to them without requiring a nurse to manually connect every step. Nurses shouldn’t have to serve as the middleware holding the communication process together.

According to recent reports, hussain: Because it adds to a load clinicians already carry. They’re surrounded by beeps, pings, messages and alerts, and most of it does not need action. The requirement to still read these messages and make that decision adds to cognitive overload and burnout.

Industry observers note that it’s a thousand small interruptions compounded by the need to choose which tool to use to communicate. And the risk goes beyond burnout. When people tune out the noise, a real emergency can slip past. That’s a patient safety issue.

FH: Why do some organizations not have clear communication rules?

Manuel: Communication practices often evolve over time as organizations grow, add new technology and adapt workflows across different departments and care teams. That can naturally lead to different ways of communicating depending on the team, the workflow or even the situation. The important thing is establishing clear communication standards and governance around those practices.

According to recent reports, hussain: Many hospitals do not have clear communication rules because communication has evolved department by department and tool by tool, rather than as an enterprise-wide workflow strategy. Health systems have invested in a lot of technology, but more technology has not always translated into more coordinated care. The result is that a nurse, physician or operator may have to decide which system to use, who to contact, how urgent the problem is and what to do if there is no response. That is a lot of operational burden being pushed onto clinicians.

Clear communication rules are notable, but they also have to be supported by technology that can operationalize those rules in real time.

FH: As messaging providers has become more commonplace at health systems, some have begun to charge for the service. How has that impacted overload, if at all?

Manuel: Research has shown that charging for certain patient messages can reduce message volume, but I don’t think we can assume that fewer messages automatically translates to less burden for clinicians.

It has been revealed that we also have to consider the potential impact on patient access. We don’t want patients hesitating to reach out with questions or concerns because they’re unsure whether they’ll be charged. From a clinical perspective, the bigger question is whether we’re reducing the work associated with managing communication. If clinicians are still sorting through unnecessary messages, tracking down information or following up on requests that weren’t routed appropriately, we haven’t really addressed the underlying burden.

Charging may influence volume, but improving how communication is managed is what can make a meaningful difference.

FH: How does message overload ultimately affect patient experience and engagement?

In a recent development, manuel: When we talk about message overload, I think the impact on patients is really about whether communication is helping care move forward or creating additional work and delays. When information is clear, actionable, and reaches the right person at the right time, clinicians can make decisions faster, reduce unnecessary delays, and keep care moving forward. When communication becomes fragmented or creates unnecessary noise, it can have the opposite effect.

Communication is also an important part of patient engagement. Patients want to understand what’s happening with their care, have their questions answered, and feel involved in decisions. When communication processes work well, clinicians have more time for those meaningful interactions and to apply their clinical judgment where it’s needed most. There’s also an element of confidence and trust. Patients may not see all of the communication happening behind the scenes, but they experience the result of it. When the care team is aligned, information is consistent, and next steps are clear, patients have greater confidence in their care and a better understanding of what to expect.

FH: How can leadership change communication without disrupting patient care?

In a recent development, hussain: Leadership can start by treating communication as a patient-care-affecting workflow, not just a technology or etiquette opportunity. The goal is not to slow communication down or create more rules for clinicians to remember. The goal is to make communication more reliable so [that] the right information reaches the right person with the right level of urgency. That requires involving frontline clinicians, understanding where delays and interruptions are happening, and then standardizing the workflows that create the most friction. Done well, this should reduce disruption because clinicians are no longer forced to manually manage every handoff, escalation, or follow-up themselves.

FH: More broadly, what can hospitals and health systems do to mitigate this overload?

In a recent development, hussain: Hospitals and health systems need to look at overload as a coordination problem. Clinicians are receiving messages, alerts, alarms and requests from many different systems, but those systems often are not working together. The first step is understanding where volume is coming from and which communications are truly actionable. From there, organizations can clarify escalation paths, reduce duplicative tools, and route communication based on role, schedule, urgency and context. Technology can help, but only if it is designed around the workflow.

FH: How could AI or other kinds of health tech provide relief for clinicians?

According to recent reports, hussain: AI and health tech can provide relief when they are built into real clinical workflows, not layered on top of them as another tool to manage. Clinicians do not need more alerts, inboxes or systems to check. They need technology that can reduce noise, understand urgency, identify the right person, and help activate the next step without forcing nurses, physicians or operators to manually coordinate it all.

Sources indicate that this is where communication orchestration matters. The goal, and much of the work we focus on at TigerConnect, is to help health systems move from fragmented communication to smarter, role-based workflows that reach the right person at the right time. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment.
  • It has been revealed that researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup.
  • Two of the new studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment. The findings, which will be presented at Neuroscience 2026, reveal important differences that could help researchers develop more personalized approaches to treating complex brain conditions. Neuroscience 2026 is the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and the world's largest source of emerging news about brain science and health.

It has been revealed that researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup. Understanding these differences could lead to treatments better suited to each individual's biology. Two conditions receiving particular attention are Alzheimer's disease (AD), an incurable disorder that progressively damages memory and other brain functions, and fibromyalgia, a chronic illness marked by persistent pain and fatigue that affects 2-4% of the global population. According to the World Health Organization, Alzheimer's affects between 35 and 40 million people worldwide.

Menopause, Genetics, and Alzheimer's Disease.

Two of the new studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.

One investigation found that people carrying genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's responded differently to menopause hormone therapy (MHT) compared with those without the same genetic risks. The effects also varied according to the particular combination of hormones used. These findings suggest that both genetic background and hormone therapy formulation deserve consideration when evaluating treatment options. (Mateja Perović, University of Toronto).

A separate study examined rodents undergoing menopause that also carried genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's. Researchers observed that brain circuits responsible for memory became particularly vulnerable, providing evidence that menopause may represent an important period of increased susceptibility for women who are genetically predisposed to the disease. (Stephanie M. Perez, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio).

Sex Differences in Chronic Pain and Brain Inflammation.

The other two studies explored how biological sex influences pain sensitivity, immune activity, and the effects of inflammation on the brain.

It has been revealed that in a mouse model of fibromyalgia, females continued to show heightened sensitivity to touch and stronger immune system activation compared with males. The findings suggest that the biological processes contributing to chronic pain may differ between sexes, potentially making treatments tailored to these differences more effective. (Yasmin Sahlloul, University of Cincinnati).

Another investigation uncovered differences in how prolonged intestinal inflammation influences the brain. Using a mouse model, researchers found that chronic gut inflammation affected brain function and Alzheimer's related disease changes differently in males and females. The results provide additional evidence that biological sex may influence the relationship between inflammation and neurological disease. (Nurcan Kilic, University of North Dakota).

Toward More Personalized Treatments for Brain Disorders.

In a recent development, together, the four studies underscore the importance of examining sex and genetic differences when investigating neurological conditions. By identifying biological factors that influence disease progression and treatment responses, researchers hope to move toward more precise therapies for Alzheimer's, fibromyalgia, and other difficult-to-treat brain disorders.

"These four studies illustrate the fascinating discoveries that can be made when focusing on female-specific biology or possible sex differences in AD-related symptoms and risk factors," said Liisa Galea, PhD, Treliving Family Chair in Women's Mental Health at Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and moderator of the press conference. "The research presented at Neuroscience 2026 helps us pinpoint the specific differences that may help us develop more targeted treatment using precision approaches, even for some of our most complex brain disorders.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

All season long, the "Dancing with the Stars" judges recognized Amber Glenn's competitive nature, but now that the season has come to an end, the Olympic figure skater is proving that she has been a team player all along.

Glen came in second place in the competition dance series, with two-time Paralympian Ezra Frech taking home the coveted Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy.

And while the contestants share a spot on Team USA—for which they've both brought home gold medals—they swiftly bonded in the competition as their professional dance partners, Pasha Pashkov and Daniella Karagach, are married.

When asked how she felt about the results after the finale, Glenn told Extra she "couldn't ask for a better result," and described a "triumphant feeling" as she walked away from Season 35 having earned 10s across the board in all three of her final performances.

"From day one, we all met up, had a little dinner over at their house, and we stated, 'We wanna go 1-2,'" she explained to the outlet. "And we didn't specify, like, whatever happens, happens, but the fact that we came in here and we both got those perfect scores. We both did everything we could and it was truly in the hands of the people at home. I'm really proud of what we did and I'm really, really happy that Team USA took it home.".

Recent findings suggest that the group—who have been unofficially dubbed "Team USA and the Pashkovs" by fans and even the official U.S. Olympic and Paralmypic team all season—have been close collaborators throughout the competition.

Industry observers note that during the Nov. 10 episode, when teams were paired off and required to compete in two-on-two dance-offs, Glenn and Pashkov and Frech and Karagach put a friendly spin on the format by switching partners mid-choreography as they performed a Rumba to "The Boy Is Mine" by Brandy and Monica.

In a recent development, "It felt more like a team dance than anything else," Karagach told Us magazine. "We came together ,and we had the best time sharing the dance floor, and we couldn't also not end swapping partners because I've always wanted to dance with Amber, and Ezra and Pasha secretly wanted to dance with each other. So that was fun.".

In a recent development, the competitors-turned-pals took to social media to share plenty of heartwarming behind-the-scenes moments throughout the experience, providing a glimpse at what their down time is like between rehearsals. In one Sept. 18 post, Pashkov wrote, "We're a tightly-knit fam now.".

In a post-finale interview with Deadline, Glenn described the moment she had realized Frech would win. The Plano, TX native mentioned, "I don't know if I felt as many emotions watching a performance as I did when watching Ezra and Dani. It was like, at first, it's excitement. I'm like, 'I love that Linkin Park [song].' And then horror, fear, and like, panic.'".

The moment Glenn was referring to was the malfunction in which Frech's prosthetic fell off mid-performance. Frech and Karagach swiftly communicated while dancing, allowing him to secure it into place properly and complete the routine.

Recent findings suggest that "I think I gasped so loud I threw my rib out again," Glenn continued. "So then, the physical pain and just like, fear, panic, and then just awe, inspiration, something you feel in your core. I know that's a saying, but like you feel it in your gut, and it takes your breath away, and that's what it was.".

Glenn noted that in that moment, she "was like, 'They won.'" She even added that she "would feel bad" if she had taken home the trophy after seeing Frech and Karagach pull off "such a perfect dance" after "working so hard for it all season.".

#146250. Latest Update: Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought

Latest Update: Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the heart gets older, inflammation increases, but scientists have not fully understood where these changes occur or which parts of the organ are most affected.
  • In a study of mouse hearts published in Aging Cell, the researchers discovered that signs of inflammation and tissue scarring were especially concentrated around the aortic valves and aortic root.
  • Recent findings suggest that "Some of the markers associated with inflammaging were there from the very beginning in young hearts, but they were focused specifically in areas no one had defined before, in the valves and the aorta rather than in muscle tissue," noted study author Nadia Rosenthal, scientific director at JAX.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the heart gets older, inflammation increases, but scientists have not fully understood where these changes occur or which parts of the organ are most affected. Researchers at The Jackson Laboratory (JAX) have now uncovered a surprising pattern: Certain regions of the heart appear to be hotspots for aging-related inflammation, offering newly introduced clues about how the heart changes over time.

In a study of mouse hearts published in Aging Cell, the researchers discovered that signs of inflammation and tissue scarring were especially concentrated around the aortic valves and aortic root. These areas contain immune cells and connective tissue cells whose interactions change with age, potentially affecting the surrounding heart muscle. The findings provide a new picture of cardiac aging and could guide future efforts to understand cardiovascular disease.

Recent findings suggest that "Some of the markers associated with inflammaging were there from the very beginning in young hearts, but they were focused specifically in areas no one had defined before, in the valves and the aorta rather than in muscle tissue," noted study author Nadia Rosenthal, scientific director at JAX. "We really have to think of aging as something that is not linear, because just like we know that people don't age at the same rate, what we know now is that organs and tissues don't age at the same rate either, even within one individual.".

Much of the previous research on heart aging has centered on cardiac muscle, particularly the left ventricle. This chamber performs the essential task of pumping blood into the aorta and throughout the body. By studying the heart as a whole, rather than concentrating primarily on its muscle, the JAX team uncovered notable changes in other tissues and the ways their cells interact.

"The valves and the major blood vessels are parts often thought of as plumbing rather than the main engine, but this is a very complicated little machine," Rosenthal said. "It turns out they're home to many of the cells we're interested in, and that's where some of the most notable aging-related signals were concentrated.".

Mapping Hidden Hotspots of Heart Aging.

Growing older is the single greatest risk factor for cardiovascular disease, yet many of the cellular processes responsible for the heart's decline remain poorly understood. One challenge is that mammalian heart muscle cells have very little ability to regenerate or replace themselves. To investigate what happens as the heart ages, Rosenthal and her colleagues used advanced techniques that allowed them to study thousands of individual cells from young and old mice while also identifying their locations within the heart.

Sources indicate that scientists already know that aging is accompanied by a persistent, low level of inflammation throughout the body. Earlier studies have found similar changes in the heart, including an increase in immune cells that regulate inflammatory activity (macrophages) and cells that produce and maintain connective tissue and contribute to scar formation (fibroblasts).

The new analysis showed that aging macrophages became more active in genes involved in inflammation and changes to tissue structure. Fibroblasts, meanwhile, increasingly displayed molecular characteristics associated with fibrosis (or scarring). Crucially, the researchers went beyond identifying which genes were active. They also mapped the locations of these cells, making it possible to see how different regions of the heart change as they grow older.

This approach revealed that inflammation and fibrosis (or scarring) were not distributed uniformly. Instead, the strongest signals appeared around the heart valves and aortic root. The researchers believe these regions may act as key centers of cardiac aging, where changes in supporting cells could influence the health of nearby heart muscle.

Sources indicate that "To keep muscle cells happy, the other cells in the heart have to continue supporting them throughout life," Rosenthal mentioned. "What this study does, for the first time, is provide a comprehensive picture of how those support cells, particularly fibroblasts and macrophages, change with age and contribute to what we call inflammaging.".

Surprising Signs of Aging in Young Hearts.

According to recent reports, another unexpected discovery challenged assumptions about how scientists identify aging cells. The team examined molecular markers frequently associated with cellular senescence, a state in which cells permanently lose the ability to divide, often because of aging or stress. As senescent cells accumulate, they can contribute to ongoing inflammation, tissue damage, and diseases associated with older age.

It has been revealed that surprisingly, some of these supposedly age-related markers were already present in young mouse hearts. Their presence suggests that the markers alone cannot reliably establish whether a cell has entered senescence, and that their meaning may depend on where they appear and the condition of the surrounding tissue.

It has been revealed that "What surprised us was that some of these markers that have been associated with aging were already present in young hearts. They weren't where anyone expected to find them, and that forced us to rethink what those markers are telling us," Rosenthal noted. "That turns the usual interpretation of cardiac aging on its ear because these markers alone don't mean a cell is senescent. There's nothing senescent about a six-month-old mouse heart.".

In a recent development, the researchers also identified genes that became more active with age and were especially prominent in the same regions. Among them were Ccl8, which helps transmit inflammatory signals, and Cdkn1a (also known as p21), a gene widely used as an indicator of cellular senescence. Their locations provided further evidence that the valves and aortic root may be particularly important areas for understanding how the heart ages.

"We're not talking about single genes. We're talking about an entire conversation between immune cells and fibroblasts. As the heart ages, the way those cells communicate changes, and that shift appears to be linked to the inflammation and tissue remodeling we see in older hearts," Rosenthal said.

Male and Female Hearts Show Different Aging Patterns.

The study uncovered another important distinction: Aging did not produce exactly the same molecular changes in male and female mouse hearts.

It has been revealed that in males, aging fibroblasts highlighted stronger connections to biological processes associated with fibrosis. In females, the corresponding changes were more closely related to pathways involved in heart development and protein production.

Rosenthal noted that these differences may offer clues about cardiovascular aging in humans. Heart disease tends to become more common in women after menopause, while its development in men generally follows a more gradual pattern. The distinct cellular changes observed in male and female mice could help researchers investigate the biological processes behind these differences.

In a recent development, however, the results describe differences in molecular activity, not demonstrated differences in heart function or disease risk. Further research will be needed to determine how these patterns influence cardiovascular health.

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the team compared the mouse results with previously published data from human hearts. Several molecular processes associated with aging, including pathways involved in responding to cellular stress, appeared in both species. This overlap suggests that at least some of the biological changes identified in mice may also be relevant to human heart aging.

"Our findings change the focus from aging across the entire heart to specific anatomical hotspots, helping us better understand how inflammation and fibrosis are connected and which regions of the heart are involved in the aging process," mentioned study author Amalia Sintou, a postdoctoral associate at JAX.

Could These Discoveries Help Protect Aging Hearts?

In a recent development, although the research does not yet identify a newly introduced treatment, it offers scientists a more detailed understanding of where aging-related changes occur and which cells are involved. By revealing these cellular patterns, the findings could help guide future studies aimed at reducing cardiovascular decline, maintaining healthy heart function, and improving health later in life.

It has been revealed that rosenthal's team is now examining whether exercise, diet, and disease alter the interactions between immune cells and connective tissue cells. The researchers hope to distinguish the normal effects of aging from changes that may leave the heart increasingly vulnerable to cardiovascular problems.

The experimental design also helped the team isolate aging itself as a contributing factor. Because the mice lived under the same conditions and received the same diet, the researchers could investigate age-related changes without the additional variation introduced by different environments or eating habits.

Sources indicate that "Valve replacement is common in older adults, and one of the big questions is how much of the underlying damage is driven by aging itself," said study author Aleksandra Aljakna Khan, a postdoctoral associate at JAX. "Because all of the mice in our study lived in the same environment and ate the same diet, we were able to isolate the effects of aging and show that aging alone can initiate some of these changes in the valves and aorta.".

It has been revealed that together, the findings suggest that understanding heart aging requires looking beyond the muscle responsible for pumping blood. The valves, major blood vessels, and supporting cells may play a much larger role than previously recognized. Learning how these structures change and communicate over time could eventually help scientists identify ways to preserve cardiovascular health as people age.

Research Funding and Study Authors.

Recent findings suggest that the research received funding from the NIH Common Fund through The Jackson Laboratory Senescence Tissue Mapping Center (JAX-Sen TMC U54 AG079753). Additional support came from JAX's National Cancer Institute-designated Cancer Center (P30 CA034196).

Additional authors from The Jackson Laboratory included Yue Zhao, Antonios Somarakis, Harshpreet Chandok, Juliana Alcoforado Diniz, Ramalakshmi Ramasamy, Gretchen T. Clark, Brian S. White, Paul Robson, Ron Korstanje, and J. Matthew Mahoney. Leon Frommer and Sikander Hayat of RWTH Aachen University also contributed to the study.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Court strikes down anti-trans Ryan White funding rules 'based in animus, loathing and discrimination'" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Medical associations and providers notched a legal victory over the federal government in a court ruling vacating federal funding requirements for Ryan White clinics involving gender-affirming care.

Those restrictions would have required recipients of Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program funds to not acknowledge the identities of transgender patients or use funds for gender-affirming care.

It was challenged by the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (HIVMA), the American Academy of HIV Medicine and the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care in June (see that coverage below), who argued that the policy was contrary to Congress' intent when establishing the program under law in 1991, lacked sufficient explanation and discriminated against transgender people in violation of the First and Fifth Amendments.

In a recent development, the Nov. 19 decision from Judge William G. Young, of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, prohibits the government from opposing its conditions in regard to all federal funding and permanently blocks any similar policies from being implemented by associational plaintifs' members, "which covers virtually every HIV care provider in the United States," mentioned Lambda Legal, which acted as co-counsel for the plaintiffs.

"The ruling is a decisive and important victory for transgender people with HIV and protects the ability of physicians and other health care professionals to offer evidence-based care without political interference," Philip Bolduc, M.D., chair of HIVMA, remarked in a statement reacting to the decision.

Young's opinion and order opened with an acknowledgement that there are "sincere and deeply felt views" regarding transgender identity, and that the issue at question was of legal regulation rather than "the propriety of individual gender expression.".

Industry observers note that still, the judge concluded his opinion by writing that the administration's conditions "are based in animus, loathing and discrimination. They do not stand for justice—in fact, they defy it. They are contrary to the laws of this nation and cannot continue to stand.".

A group of medical associations and providers has filed a lawsuit challenging new federal funding requirements for Ryan White clinics involving gender-affirming care.

The new requirements, issued in a recent HRSA Notice of Funding Opportunity, require recipients of the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program funds to not acknowledge the identities of transgender patients or use funds for gender-affirming care. The restrictions undermine the very intent of the program, the plaintiffs say, and violate anti-discrimination components of the Fifth Amendment.

“The Ryan White Program was created as a public health intervention to address the needs of low-income, vulnerable populations who otherwise would not have access to life-saving care,” Melanie Thompson, M.D., co-chair of a primary care guidance panel for the HIV Medicine Association, noted in a press release. “It is crucial that Ryan White clinicians be allowed to continue to deliver the most scientifically appropriate treatments for all patients, including transgender individuals, without discrimination if we are to improve health outcomes for all and end the U.S. HIV epidemic.".

Recent findings suggest that the lawsuit alleges (PDF) that HHS and HRSA violated the Administrative Procedure Act by exceeding their statutory authority and imposing restrictions that conflict with the Ryan White statute. The plaintiffs ask the court to block enforcement of the funding restrictions.

The case was filed by Lambda Legal and HSF Kramer on behalf of the American Academy of HIV Medicine, the HIV Medicine Association and the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care, plus two providers.

In a recent development, A preliminary hearing will likely be scheduled in a few weeks. Lambda Legal is “cautiously optimistic” about the future of the case, José Abrigo, senior attorney and HIV project director at Lambda Legal, told reporters on a webinar on Thursday afternoon. He called the administration’s actions “unlawful,” and noted gender-affirming care in this context includes all types of care, including primary care and mental healthcare.

Specifically, the HRSA Notice of Funding Opportunity reads: “Discretionary awards shall not be used to fund, promote, encourage, subsidize, or facilitate … denial by the recipient of the sex binary in humans, or the belief that sex is a chosen or mutable characteristic.”.

Sources indicate that some providers are already preemptively complying with the restrictions, Abrigo said, particularly in Tennessee and Kentucky. It is unclear how many other providers will also stop gender-affirming care. In certain cases, it’s up to individual states or departments of health to enforce the restrictions. It’s possible that medical records could be audited and reviewed for indications of pronouns, per Thompson. “It does matter what someone’s gender and pronouns are listed as,” Thompson said on the webinar, explaining that medical records are shared between providers and help ensure affirming care.

Sources indicate that if a clinic is found to be non-compliant, the repercussions are steep, Thompson added. “The penalty for being found out is severe, and puts an entire program’s funding in jeopardy,” she noted on the webinar.

Forty percent of American Academy of HIV Medicine members rely on Ryan White funding, of which 40% voluntarily report providing gender-affirming medical care. For low-income trans individuals with HIV, there aren’t many alternative options, per Abrigo. They may seek care through private insurance or potentially through Medicaid, but typically the population relies on Ryan White clinics for services.

Gender-affirming care restrictions under the Trump administration have been commonplace. Over 40 hospitals have reportedly stopped some gender-affirming care services for minors in response to pressure. Last week, the Cleveland Clinic promised the Department of Justice (DOJ) to commit $2 million to detransitioning services and a “decades-long” agreement not to perform gender-affirming care on minors. Delivering most of these services is currently illegal for minors under Ohio state law. Last month, DOJ struck a similar deal with Texas Children’s.

According to recent reports, for months, experts have been sounding the alarm about the U.S. HIV response slipping into dangerous instability. In April, the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care (IAPAC) released a data brief finding that 61% of providers have reported at least one HIV service disruption and 68% have seen operational changes such as staffing reductions, service cutbacks and program closures. This was attributed to a combination of policy decisions, funding cuts and social determinants like loss of insurance coverage.

“It’s a catastrophe in the making," José M. Zúñiga, AIPAC's president and CEO, told reporters on the webinar. "It was already happening. This adds fuel.".

Tech Report: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open newly introduced possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders.
  • The findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins.
  • Sources indicate that mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open newly introduced possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders. Researchers found that the vitamin can correct developmental problems in tiny worms carrying a genetic mutation associated with Verheij syndrome, a rare human condition that causes developmental delays, impaired growth, and short stature.

The findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins. During splicing, unnecessary portions of messenger RNA are removed, and the remaining sections are joined together in the correct order. When this process goes wrong, it can disrupt essential cellular functions and contribute to serious developmental disorders.

Sources indicate that mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome. To better understand the effects of these genetic changes, scientists investigated how a related mutation affects growth and metabolism in a laboratory model.

Vitamin B12 Reverses Developmental Defects in Worms.

According to recent reports, the discovery emerged from experiments involving C. elegans, a tiny roundworm commonly used in biological research. The researchers were initially searching for previously unknown genes that influence lifespan when they began examining a mutation in a gene involved in RNA splicing. The same gene is associated with Verheij syndrome in humans.

It has been revealed that worms carrying the mutation developed problems resembling important features of the human disorder. Their growth slowed considerably, and they remained smaller than normal.

To investigate why this happened, the scientists conducted genetic screens and analyzed the worms' metabolism. They discovered that the mutation disrupted specific metabolic pathways that depend on vitamin B12 and are essential for healthy growth and normal cellular activity.

Industry observers note that the researchers then tested whether providing additional vitamin B12 could counteract these changes. Remarkably, the treatment restored the affected metabolic processes to normal and corrected the developmental abnormalities associated with the mutation.

According to recent reports, "We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism," notes Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. "Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12.".

Could Vitamin B12 Help Treat a Rare Genetic Disorder?

It has been revealed that to explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the researchers examined publicly available datasets from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at the University Hospital Cologne, to collect blood samples from patients diagnosed with Verheij syndrome.

These investigations uncovered evidence of similar metabolic changes in humans, suggesting that the vitamin B12-related pathways affected in the worms may also play a role in the human disorder.

Although the results are promising, researchers have not yet established whether vitamin B12 supplementation can improve symptoms in people with Verheij syndrome. Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether the benefits observed in worms can be translated into a treatment for patients.

The discovery also raises a broader possibility. Metabolic disruptions may contribute more substantially to diseases caused by faulty RNA splicing than scientists previously recognized. Understanding these connections could help researchers identify fresh therapeutic strategies, potentially extending beyond Verheij syndrome to other rare genetic conditions.

In a recent development, "Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide fresh insights into human diseases," states Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. "A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term.".
