Florida sues The Leapfrog Group for 'misrepresenting' its hospital safety grades to consumers" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Florida’s attorney general has filed a lawsuit against hospital safety watchdog The Leapfrog Group alleging that it misled consumers about how it determines the grades assigned to hospitals, particularly those that declined to voluntarily submit data to the group.

The complaint, which was filed late last week and lists President and CEO Leah Binder alongside her organization, follows a similar suit brought by Tenet hospitals in the state that convinced a judge that nonparticipating hospitals were being “unfairly” penalized in Leapfrog’s methodology.

It has been revealed that the group was ordered to withhold safety grades for those hospitals and in grade releases since has voluntarily chosen not to award ratings to hundreds of others that did not submit recent quality data to its surveys. Leapfrog appealed that decision in September, and has remarked it is reviewing a potential methodology change for upcoming gradings to incorporate non-submitting hospitals.

The Florida Office of Attorney General James Uthmeier’s lawsuit cites that case. It argues that Leapfrog’s poor scores for “at least seven Florida hospitals” misled patients, and outlined specific cases in which patients had declined care over the perceived poor performances of those hospitals.

According to recent reports, “The Leapfrog Group told Florida patients its hospital grades were peer-reviewed and backed by experts. That was a lie,” Uthmeier mentioned in a Friday release announcing the litigation. “When hospitals declined to fill out its survey, Leapfrog handed them the worst scores in the country without a shred of data, and patients refused surgery because of it. Leapfrog and its CEO should expect to be held accountable.”.

The office requested that the court permanently bar Leapfrog from “misrepresenting to Florida consumers … the data, sources, methods or expert approvals underlying any hospital grade or score they publish,” or from representing the scores as peer reviewed. It also seeks to limit Leapfrog’s solicitation of charitable contributions, make corrective disclosures, and pay out other relief to providers, patients or other affected individuals and groups.

Leapfrog, in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, said the office’s case “poses the specter of outright government censorship,” and was “piggybacking” on the Tenet hospitals’ case “with old allegations Leapfrog strongly refuted.”.

Sources indicate that “Leapfrog looks forward to answering in court and defending our First Amendment rights and most importantly, patient safety,” the group’s statement reads. “Too many patients are harmed or killed by medical errors and infections in hospitals, and Leapfrog will always stand up for their lives as we have for 26 years.”.

The methodology change at the heart of the cases came ahead of Leapfrog’s fall 2024 safety grade publication. It more heavily weighed “imputed” scores for four of Leapfrog’s 32 safety measures that were assigned when recent safety data for the two preceding years were unavailable. The Tenet hospitals, in their case, highlighted internal communications and other testimony that questioned the validity of the changes. Both lawsuits suggest the changes were made to maximize hospital participation in Leapfrog’s survey, which would bring downstream increases to revenues it collects from allowing hospitals to advertise their grades.

Uthmeier’s office has also filed a friend of the court brief to the appellate court now considering Leapfrog’s appeal, where it similarly argues that Leapfrog’s conduct is a violation of Florida’s consumer protection laws and not protected by the First Amendment.

The fresh complaint comes the same week as Leapfrog’s latest hospital safety grade release, which, similar to the spring release, withheld grades for 447 hospitals.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In a recent development, in recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing newly introduced opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

Industry observers note that with digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Industry observers note that even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Sources indicate that another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

In a recent development, finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech organization could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With housing costs skyrocketing, every little bit helps—and sometimes, there are options even longtime homeowners are unaware of.

Recent findings suggest that for example, a homeowner recently turned to Reddit to vent about humidity and outdoor air entering their home. They received quotes for an energy audit ranging from $100 to $200 and asked if this service is actually worth it.

Someone from Connecticut replied saying they paid only $50 for the same type of audit, thanks to a subsidy from their electric company—and depending on your location, utility provider, and/or income, you could also qualify for a subsidized or even free energy audit.

It has been revealed that while experts agree that a $50 assessment is less common, even paying a few hundred for one may save you thousands of dollars down the road. That's because it can uncover hidden air leaks that may contribute to higher utility bills and damaging moisture issues.

Recent findings suggest that “When you seal air leaks, you may prevent water vapor inside your house from turning into liquid inside your walls. This eliminates the need for costly wood rot and mold problems that may lead to $5,000 or more in repairs and reduces wear and tear on your HVAC unit,” explains Andrew Pho, a home renovation and improvement expert at Mister Balustealing in Toronto.

Energy audits are designed to find what’s causing energy loss in your home, but they’re not all created equal.

Before booking one, confirm what it includes.

“At the very least, it should consist of a blower-door test (a blower fan is set up in a doorway to measure how much air is leaking in or out of the home), check the levels of insulation in your attic, walls, etc., and look at your HVAC system to make sure it’s running efficiently,” notes Dennis Vong, founder and owner of Inland Power Wash in Orange County, CA.

Clear, written suggestions on how to improve the energy efficiency of your home are important as well.

“Additionally, you may want to ask if minor fixes like caulking and weatherstripping are included in the audit or available for an additional cost,” Vong explains.

Niki O'Brien, operations manager at Custom Exteriors in Loveland, CO, reinforces the importance of ensuring your home has proper insulation and ventilation in your attic.

“It can prevent dangerous freeze/thaw cycles that can trap moisture and lead to ice damming and interior leaks,” O’Brien claims.

If your goal is to improve energy efficiency and reduce the risk of needing repairs, an energy audit is a good idea.

According to Energy Star, proper insulation and air sealing can cut your heating and cooling bills by as much as 15% on average.

“If you spend $200 a month on heating and cooling, that could mean savings of about $30 a month, or $360 a year,” Vong explains.

O’Brien has experienced the benefits of an energy audit firsthand.

“We have seen many cases, including a home we owned personally, that needed additional insulation and resulted in lower energy costs,” notes O’Brien.

At the end of the day, the information you get from an energy audit will absolutely save you money in the long run.

“Whether that means getting newly introduced, energy-efficient products, adding additional weather proofing to existing systems, or repairing/replacing caulking, insulation, or creating effective ventilation, eventually it will surpass the cost of an audit,” O’Brien adds.

Industry observers note that according to the Department of Energy, an energy audit will typically run you between $250 and $600. The good news is you may be able to get one at a subsidized rate.

“I recommend calling your gas and electric providers to see if they offer energy audits at a subsidized rate and what rebates may be available if you were to make any energy improvements to your home,” notes Vong.

Aaron Christy, founder and owner of Indy Roof & Restoration in Indianapolis, indicates that in Indianapolis, for example, AES Indiana offers all of its customers a no-cost virtual assessment, and a free in-home assessment if you meet certain income limits.

Your state may also offer a no-cost assessment.

“In my state, Massachusetts, there’s the Mass Save Program, which provides free audits to qualifying homeowners, renters, and landlords,” explains Ted Dow, vice president of delivery at Power Home Remodeling in Boston.

While you’re waiting for an audit, you can perform your own DIY assessment.

Make sure the weatherstripping around your doors and windows isn’t falling apart, check for any dripping faucets or leaking pipes, and make sure your gutters are draining properly away from your foundation.

“Just remember that it’s best to leave the more specialized services to the pros,” adds Vong.

Unpacking the implications from CMS' latest proposed Medicare Advantage changes" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Late last week, the Trump administration released a proposed rule that includes a slew of technical changes in Medicare Advantage for 2028, citing enhanced competition as a key goal.

Analysts dove into the beefy regulation and projected that changes to MA's star ratings program would likely cull more than $100 billion in federal spending over the next decade.

Per a note from Leerink Partners, estimates from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services suggest that the changes would cut federal spending by $11.5 billion in 2031 and $107 billion through 2037.

The Leerink analysts estimate that about 58% of Medicare Advantage contracts would see lower scores using the newly proposed methodology, with about 20% of contracts losing quality bonus payments, which are tied to star ratings performance.

In the rule, CMS proposed moving to a set of 15 measures to determine the star ratings scores, which are focused on member experience and outcomes. The proposed rule would also eliminate the Reward Factor, and in tandem, these changes "would remove a cushion for contracts sitting at the critical QBP threshold, while concentrating performance across fewer measures," according to the Leerink report.

The analysts said that the potential impact of these proposals "reminds us just how many looks have been living at 4 stars for years with the hugely key Reward Factor.".

The report estimates that the changes to the star ratings, if finalized, would have an uneven impact on insurers. For example, Humana would see the number of contracts earning four or more stars decline from 95% to 82.9%. Clover Health, meanwhile, would likely maintain 100% of its contracts, earning at least four stars.

According to recent reports, unitedHealthcare, by comparison, could see a drop from having 67.9% of its contracts in looks with at least four stars in 2027 to just 8.8% under the new methodology. For Aetna, the Leerink analysts project a decrease from 70% to 0%.

Recent findings suggest that given the scale of the changes, the Leerink analysts write that the rule sets the stage for a significant overhaul of the policies and rules that govern Medicare Advantage. The proposal is "almost overwhelming in size, scope and the impact on the industry.".

Molly Turco, a policy analyst at TD Cowen, wrote in a note Monday that the proposed rule "is more significant than expected, in both revenue impact and scope and touches most core aspects of MA.".

"It appears CMS aimed to reform long-standing concerns, especially Stars, in a way that takes money out of the program, while also loosening regulation on things like agents/brokers, seamless enrollment, network adequacy, etc. to help the program grow," Turco wrote. "However, we think these growth/deregulation policies are unlikely to offset the headwinds for MA.".

She noted that while most of the most painful changes wouldn't impact looks until 2031 at the earliest; the delay does suggest CMS may be comfortable including more significant short-term changes to risk adjustment in the forthcoming 2028 Advance Notice, which is expected in January.

Ryan Langston, an equity research analyst at TD Cowen, wrote in the note that the proposed rule would likely be net negative for insurers with large, multi-state contracts and more people enrolled with aims earning at least four stars.

According to recent reports, the delayed timeline of at least four years does grant intends time to adapt, Langston wrote, but the financial impacts would likely force benefit changes. The proposed rule could also spook investors concerned about what's included in the 2028 rate notice, he said.

"The combination of a smaller measure set, elimination of reward factors and reduced improvement measure protection likely lower Star ratings across the industry and force plans to mitigate lost revenue via benefit revisions," Langston wrote.

The Leerink analysts wrote that health aims are almost certain to fight the regulation. Lawsuits have become commonplace in the stars space, with multiple payers suing the feds over the most recent round of scores.

"We believe a lot of what has been proposed will change and/or not be implemented at all," they wrote. "Expect industry litigation.".

Upcoming wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new wearable patch could offer a surprisingly simple way to improve one of the most crucial stages of sleep, without relying on medication or surgery.
  • Known as NEUSLeeP, the soft patch attaches to the skin and combines ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that monitor brain activity in real time.
  • REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement sleep, is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new wearable patch could offer a surprisingly simple way to improve one of the most crucial stages of sleep, without relying on medication or surgery. Developed by researchers led by the University of Texas at Austin, the device uses gentle ultrasound waves to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, helping people enter REM sleep sooner and spend more time in this restorative stage.

Known as NEUSLeeP, the soft patch attaches to the skin and combines ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that monitor brain activity in real time. This allows researchers to influence brain regions involved in sleep while simultaneously tracking how the brain responds.

REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement sleep, is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs. It also plays an important role in processing emotions, consolidating memories, and adapting to stress. Disturbances in this stage of sleep have been associated with several mental health conditions, making it an important target for new treatments.

It has been revealed that "This is the first time we've been able to noninvasively target deep brain regions involved in REM sleep, while simultaneously monitoring brain activity," stated Kai Wing "Kevin" Tang, a recent UT biomedical engineering Ph.D. graduate who led the research effort.

"Our skin-attached NEUSLeeP patch opens up new possibilities for understanding sleep and treating sleep disorders in home settings," added Huiliang "Evan" Wang, assistant professor in the Cockrell School of Engineering's Department of Biomedical Engineering. Wang supervised Tang's research and served as the principal investigator (PI) overseeing the project.

Sleep Patch Helps People Reach REM Sleep 43 Minutes Faster.

The early results suggest that the technology can make a measurable difference in how people experience REM sleep.

In a study involving 28 participants, published in Nature Communications, people using the patch entered REM sleep an average of 43 minutes sooner and spent approximately 16 additional minutes in that stage.

It has been revealed that these improvements were observed in both healthy sleepers and participants experiencing certain sleep difficulties. The volunteers also reported that the patch was comfortable to wear, with minimal adverse effects.

Sources indicate that unlike medications that affect the body more broadly, NEUSLeeP is designed to deliver stimulation to specific brain regions involved in sleep regulation. It uses ultrasound, a form of sound energy with frequencies beyond human hearing, to reach areas beneath the surface of the brain without requiring an invasive procedure.

The findings are encouraging, although the relatively small study means that larger trials will be needed to determine how consistently the technology works and whether its benefits persist over time.

Potential Benefits for Stress and Emotional Health.

The researchers also found evidence that the patch's effects may extend beyond increasing REM sleep.

Industry observers note that among healthy participants, ultrasound stimulation improved heart rate variability, a measure of the natural differences in time between consecutive heartbeats. This measurement provides insight into how the body's nervous system responds to stress and adjusts to changing conditions.

Brain imaging revealed changes in neural circuits involved in emotional processing. Together, these findings suggest that improving REM sleep through targeted stimulation could potentially support emotional regulation and the ability to cope with stress.

In a recent development, "REM sleep is not just about dreaming -- it's about emotional reset and stress adaptation," explained Gregory Fonzo, assistant professor in the Dell Medical School's Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and one of the project's co-PIs. "By enhancing REM, we may help people better cope with stress and improve their overall well-being.".

These possibilities are especially interesting because REM sleep disturbances have been linked to depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

In a recent development, current approaches to sleep problems often involve medication or behavioral therapy. Although these treatments can be effective, medications may produce unwanted side effects, and existing approaches do not always directly address the biological processes responsible for disrupted REM sleep.

According to recent reports, A device capable of influencing those processes without drugs or surgery could therefore offer an additional treatment option. However, the researchers have not yet established whether NEUSLeeP can improve symptoms of mental health disorders.

A Fresh Direction for Treating Insomnia and PTSD.

Building on the initial findings, the research team prepares to conduct larger clinical trials to confirm the patch's effects and investigate its potential use in people with PTSD, depression, and chronic insomnia.

Beyond treating sleep disorders, the technology could eventually support sleep monitoring at home and provide scientists with a new way to study how deep brain regions influence sleep. Researchers also envision personalized therapies that could be adjusted to individual sleep patterns and needs.

Industry observers note that "Our vision is a future where patients with mental health disorders can optimize their sleep with a noninvasive and safe treatment," said Vincent Mysliwiec, M.D., a professor at UT Health San Antonio, a leading expert in sleep disorders, and another co-PI on the project. "This technology could help millions of people get the restorative sleep they need.".

Recent findings suggest that the team is already taking steps toward making NEUSLeeP available beyond the research setting. Working with the university's commercialization unit, Discovery to Impact, the researchers are exploring how to bring the device to market and have filed a patent application covering the technology.

If future studies confirm the early results, this wearable ultrasound patch could become a valuable fresh tool for improving REM sleep and potentially addressing conditions associated with poor sleep.

Other members of the research team include William D. Moscoso-Barrera, Mengxia Yu, Mengmeng Yao, Jinmo Jeong, Ilya Pyatnitskiy, Anakaren Romero Lozano, Jiachen Wang, Ju-Chun Hsieh, Tony Sungjin Chae, Daniel Song, Julieta Garcia, Rithvik Mittapalli, and Adam Bush of the Department of Biomedical Engineering; Benjamin Baird of the College of Natural Sciences' Department of Psychology; and Wynn Legon of Virginia Tech's Fralin Biomedical Research Institute.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
HHS: Medicaid state-directed payment savings 'primarily' stem from slowing growth" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

It has been revealed that rural hospitals claim a relatively small portion of the state-directed payments being squeezed in coming years by 2025’s H.R. 1, with much of the legislation’s projected spending reductions the result of holding funds for those hospitals from growing beyond fiscal year 2025 levels, Department of Health and Human Services policy heads wrote in a new report.

The analysis, released Monday, paints a softer picture of the rate limits Republicans imposed on a supplemental Medicaid payment stream in last year’s broad budget reconciliation law, also referred to as the One Substantial Beautiful Bill Act or the Working Families Tax Cut Legislation.

Hospitals and other healthcare industry groups, as well as advocates and Democrats, have noted the law’s billions in projected savings—from state-directed payment changes as well as other policy areas like Medicaid work requirements—are likely to devastate providers already operating at thin or negative margins.

In a recent development, specifically, the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation (ASPE)’s analysis highlighted that an estimated 7.8% of Medicaid state-directed payments reached rural hospitals in FY2025, or $11.5 billion out of $148.3 billion. That rate is slightly above rural hospitals’ 7% share of total Medicaid hospital spending for that same fiscal year, as estimated by the CMS Office of the Actuary.

Recent findings suggest that scaling from that baseline in line with H.R. 1’s multi-year payment rate phasedown, with some cumulative adjustments, highlighted that total nominal cumulative spending on rural state-directed payments would decline by 42.9%, or $81.6 billion, from 2026 through 2035 under the bill. This rate is again slightly higher than the CMS Office of the Actuary’s 40.8% estimate for all affected hospitals, which ASPE remarked is the result of the higher average dollar weighted payment rates rural hospitals right now receive, “which means that rural providers have more room to reduce rates to meet the new limits of 100% to 110% of Medicare.”.

In a recent development, the ASPE report’s bottom line, however, is that $75.2 billion of the $81.6 billion reduction rural hospitals face, or 92.1%, reflects projected increases over the FY2025 baseline of $11.5 billion. The remainder, about 7.9% of the projected change, is a reduction below FY2025’s estimated state-directed payments to rural hospitals.

HHS, in a release highlighting the report’s findings, remarked that the language used in government reports describing the full $81.6 billion 10-year spending reduction as “savings” misses the government’s primary goal of capping future growth.

“Counting every dollar of projected savings as a cut below existing funding gives the public the wrong picture. Most of these savings are not reductions below what the program spent in 2025,” HHS Chief Economist and Chief Regulatory Officer Casey Mulligan, who was one of the report’s coauthors, mentioned in the release. “They reflect future spending increases that will no longer occur. Our analysis makes that distinction clear.”.

In a recent development, H.R. 1’s multi-year scale down in state-directed payment rates is set to begin in 2028, and are expected to slash some hard-hit states’ Medicaid spending by up to a quarter of their total annual Medicaid spending, per one analysis. Hospitals have broadly criticized the policy changes while spending much of this year adjusting their operations to contend with the future limits supplemental revenue, expectations of increased uncompensated care costs and year-to-year expense pressures like wage and supply inflation.

Additionally, CMS earlier this year proposed state directed payment caps substantially more extensive than what was outlined in H.R. 1 and used as the basis for Monday’s ASPE report. That proposal would extend rate limits beyond the bill’s four outlined service areas (inpatient hospital services, outpatient hospital services, nursing facility services and qualified practitioner services at an academic medical center) to “all [state-directed payments]s for all services in all states.” Hospital groups have flatly opposed the proposal, which more than triples the 10-year estimated savings.

Recent findings suggest that lawmakers last year, when seeking votes, blunted H.R. 1's funding reductions for rural hospitals by inserting a five-year, $50 billion rural health fund into the legislation. Those funds have come with usage restrictions for states and providers, with critics also noting transparency concerns and the fund's relatively small scale compared to the bill's total projected impact on hospitals.

#146234. Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1481 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1481 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits.
  • According to recent reports, researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease.
  • According to recent reports, the results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits. Although heavy drinking was linked to worse health outcomes regardless of the beverage, the picture was more complicated among people who consumed smaller amounts of alcohol.

According to recent reports, researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease. In contrast, similar amounts of beer, cider, and spirits were linked to a higher risk. The findings, presented at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session (ACC.26), suggest that both the type and quantity of alcohol may influence its relationship with long-term health.

According to recent reports, the results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health. Importantly, the new findings do not establish that wine itself protects against disease.

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," stated Zhangling Chen, MD, PhD, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author.

How a Study of 340,000 Adults Measured Alcohol Risk.

To investigate the relationship between drinking habits and longevity, scientists examined data from 340,924 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2022. The UK Biobank is a large research resource that collects health and lifestyle information to help scientists investigate factors associated with disease and mortality.

Participants reported their alcohol consumption through dietary questionnaires when they joined the study. Researchers then classified them into four groups based on how much pure alcohol they typically consumed each day or week, rather than simply counting drinks.

This distinction matters because beer, wine, and spirits contain different concentrations of alcohol. For comparison, a 12-ounce can of beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits each provide approximately 14 grams of pure alcohol.

People consuming fewer than 20 g (about 1.5 standard drinks) per week were placed in the never or occasional drinking group. Low consumption was defined as 20 g per week up to 20 g per day for men, and 20 g per week up to 10 g per day for women.

Sources indicate that moderate drinking was defined as 20 g to 40 g (about 1.5 to three standard drinks) daily for men and 10 g to 20 g daily for women. High consumption meant more than 40 g (about three drinks) per day for men or more than 20 g (about 1.5 drinks) per day for women.

Researchers followed participants' health outcomes for an average of more than 13 years, allowing them to examine how drinking patterns were associated with deaths from different causes.

Wine, Beer, and Spirits Show Different Heart Health Risks.

Sources indicate that the clearest finding concerned heavy alcohol consumption. Compared with people who never drank or consumed alcohol only occasionally, heavy drinkers had a 24% higher risk of dying from any cause. Their risk of dying from cancer was 36% higher, while their risk of dying from heart disease was 14% higher.

These increased risks were associated with heavy drinking regardless of whether participants preferred wine, beer, cider, or spirits.

Sources indicate that however, the results became more surprising when researchers examined low and moderate alcohol consumption. At these levels, the type of beverage was associated with substantially different outcomes.

People who consumed wine in low to moderate amounts had a significantly lower risk of death, while those who consumed comparable amounts of beer, cider, or spirits had a significantly higher risk.

The contrast was especially striking for cardiovascular disease, a broad category of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than people who never or only occasionally drank alcohol.

By comparison, even low consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was associated with a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.

These percentages describe relative differences in risk between groups, not the absolute probability that an individual will die from cardiovascular disease. Because the research was observational, the findings also cannot demonstrate that choosing one alcoholic beverage over another directly changes a person's risk.

"Our findings help clarify previously mixed evidence on low to moderate alcohol consumption," Chen stated. "These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed, but also on the type of beverage. Even low to moderate intake of spirits, beer, or cider is linked to higher mortality, while low to moderate intake of wine may carry lower risk.".

Why Might Wine Be Linked to Lower Heart Risks?

Researchers identified several possible explanations for the differences, including the chemical composition of wine and the habits of people who drink it.

Red wine contains polyphenols, naturally occurring compounds found in plants that can have antioxidant properties. Antioxidants help counter certain chemical reactions involving unstable molecules that can damage cells. Some polyphenols have been investigated for potential benefits to blood vessels and cardiovascular function.

These compounds could contribute to the associations observed in wine drinkers, although the study did not establish that they were responsible for the lower mortality risk.

Another possible explanation involves how and when people drink.

Sources indicate that wine is more commonly consumed alongside meals, and wine drinkers often report healthier diets and lifestyle habits. Drinking wine may therefore be associated with other behaviors that support cardiovascular health.

In a recent development, beer, cider, and spirits, on the other hand, are more frequently consumed outside of meals. In this study, people who favored these beverages also tended to have poorer overall diet quality and other lifestyle factors associated with increased health risks.

Such differences make it difficult to separate the effects of the alcohol itself from the characteristics and habits of the people consuming it.

"Taken together, these factors suggest that the type of alcohol, how it is consumed, and the associated lifestyle behaviors all contribute to the observed differences in mortality risk," Chen noted.

What the Findings Mean for Alcohol and Health.

Sources indicate that to make their comparisons more reliable, the researchers statistically adjusted their analyses for numerous factors that might influence mortality. These included age and other demographic characteristics, socioeconomic circumstances, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic health.

Cardiometabolic factors include conditions and measurements related to heart and metabolic health, such as blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, and cholesterol levels. The analyses also accounted for family histories of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Even with these adjustments, the researchers emphasized several important limitations.

Because the study was observational, it could identify associations between alcohol consumption and mortality but could not prove that particular beverages caused better or worse outcomes. Other differences between participants may have influenced the findings despite the statistical adjustments.

Alcohol intake was also measured through questionnaires completed when participants first entered the study. That information depended on participants accurately reporting their own drinking habits, and it did not capture changes in consumption during the years that followed.

Industry observers note that another consideration is that UK Biobank participants tend to be healthier than the general population. This could limit how well the findings apply to other groups of people.

According to recent reports, the researchers suggested that high-quality randomized trials could provide stronger evidence about the health effects of different drinking patterns. Such studies would help clarify whether the observed differences reflect the beverages themselves or other factors associated with their consumption.

Nevertheless, the enormous study population and more than 13 years of average follow-up provide considerable statistical strength. By examining specific types of alcohol, different levels of consumption, and multiple causes of death, the research offers a more detailed picture of alcohol's potential health risks than many earlier investigations.

The findings highlight an crucial distinction: while heavy drinking is consistently associated with harmful health outcomes, the relationships observed at lower consumption levels may depend on beverage choice, drinking habits, and broader lifestyle patterns.

Industry observers note that for now, the apparent advantage among wine drinkers should not be interpreted as a reason to start drinking wine for heart health. The evidence points to a complex relationship between alcohol and mortality, rather than proving that any alcoholic drink offers protection.

Ziyue Li presented the study, "Alcohol Use at Mid-Life and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality," at ACC.26.

WTW: Global health insurance costs set to rise 10.2% next year" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Global health insurance costs are set to rise by double digits in 2027 for the second straight year, according to a new survey.

In a recent development, WTW released its latest Global Medical Trends Survey, which estimates that the average gross cost for medical benefits will increase by 10.2% in 2027. This follows a 10.1% increase in 2026 and a 9.8% increase in 2025, according to the report.

In the United States, the cost for medical benefits is expected to rise by 10.3% on average, on par with 2026 and up from a 9.4% increase in 2025. Across regions, the highest increases are expected in the Asia-Pacific, averaging 12.6% in 2027.

The next-highest region was North America, with a projected 10.5% average increase.

The survey was conducted in June and August 2026 and includes responses from 393 insurers offering coverage across 92 countries. Just under half (49%) of those surveyed stated they anticipate elevated medical and pharmacy costs to impact them over the next three years, and likely persist beyond that window.

The WTW analysts remarked this likely means that insurers will remain focused on cost containment and sharing measures in the near future.

"In the US, healthcare costs remain under sustained pressure from upcoming medical technologies, specialty pharmaceuticals, and the rising use of GLP-1 therapies, alongside higher provider costs and the ongoing demands of chronic and complex conditions," mentioned Courtney Stubblefield, strategy and specialty leader in Health & Benefits at WTW in an announcement.

Sources indicate that more than three quarters (76%) of the surveyed insurers named fresh medical technologies as the leading cost drive for both medical and pharmaceutical costs. Sixty-five percent cited provider fee increases, and 45% named pharmaceutical advancements.

In a recent development, cancer was the leading condition driving costs, the survey found, with 62% naming it as the top cost condition. Sixty-one percent of those surveyed said they have seen an increase in cancer diagnoses among individuals under age 40 when compared to the past two years.

However, when looking at the conditions where costs are growing the most rapidly, cardiovascular disease rises to No. 1, cited by 54% of the surveyed insurers. Cancer was second on this ranking, and named by 51%, while diabetes was third at 28%.

"To manage this, employers need a multiyear, multifaceted strategy that addresses pharmacy spending and high-cost conditions—such as cancer, cardiovascular disease and diabetes—while keeping care affordable and accessible for employees," Stubblefield stated.

UPDATED 20:54 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Rajiv Ramaswami is stepping down from his role as chief executive of Nutanix Inc., six years after he joined the hyperconverged cloud infrastructure company from its rival VMware Inc.

Recent findings suggest that in a letter to organization employees, Ramaswami (pictured) remarked he’s going to continue in the role for the time being while he works with Nutanix’s board of directors to identify a successor and assist with the transition. “After that, I will continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time,” he said in the letter.

Ramaswami, who is 60 years old, did not give any reason for his coming departure, but the letter seems to indicate that he’s not ready to retire just yet.

“Our next CEO will inherit a strong platform, a loyal customer base and, most importantly, an exceptional team,” Ramaswami wrote. “Until then, my focus remains on leading this company and nothing about our day-to-day priorities changes. I am committed to helping our next leader succeed, and my ask of you, as always, is to continue to focus on executing as we go through this leadership transition.”.

According to recent reports, ramaswami added that Nutanix has hired an executive search firm to lead the hunt for his successor. The news came as the company delivered its first-quarter earnings report, posting modest year-over-year gains in profit and revenue.

Industry observers note that the company reported adjusted earnings of 73 cents per share, beating Wall Street’s target of 61 cents per share by a strong margin. Revenue for the period came to $772.4 million, up 15% from a year earlier and above the Street’s forecast of $762.7 million.

Nutanix’s outlook for the current quarter is strong, with the company guiding for sales of between $820 million and $830 million, compared with the Street’s consensus estimate of $820.4 million. However, the full-year picture is a little less rosy, with Nutanix guiding for annual sales of $3.18 billion to $3.23 billion. The midpoint of that range trails the Street’s forecast of $3.22 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue.

According to recent reports, investors did not take the news very well. The cautious full-year guidance compared with the uncertainty over leadership prompted many to sell, and Nutanix’s stock was down 8% after-hours, having already fallen more than 5% during the regular trading session, on a down day for many tech stocks.

According to recent reports, virginia Gambale, of the board at Nutanix, hailed the “tremendous impact” Ramaswami had on the tech giant during his six-year tenure. “Rajiv led the company’s transformation to subscription software, built a loyal and expanding global enterprise base and established a technology portfolio that we believe positions us well for the AI era,” she said. “We’re focused on selecting an exceptional leader who can build on that foundation.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a conference call with analysts, Ramaswami stated he believes the company is embarking on the third major chapter in its history. The first chapter, before his arrival, saw the company establish itself as the leader of the hyperconverged infrastructure industry. Chapter two began when he took over, and saw Nutanix expand from those roots to become a platform company, he said.

Recent findings suggest that “[We have] transformed the organization to be profitable while growing and expanding the product portfolio quite significantly, from HCI to a platform that works across clouds, supports external storage and has cloud-native capabilities and now moving into the future with AI capabilities,” Ramaswami stated. “Chapter two is well-established at this point and there’s a lot of opportunity in terms of driving growth. I feel like we are in a very good place.”.

In a recent development, according to Ramaswami, Nutanix now stands at an inflection point as it looks to cash in on the upcoming era of artificial intelligence. “I’ve been talking to the board for a bit about this, as well as in terms of our strategic direction and the timing for succession, and so we came to the conclusion together that this is perhaps the right time,” he told analysts. “[We wanted] to announce it ahead of time as we look for the appropriate next leader.”.

Ramaswami’s departure from the company should at least be a lot smoother than his arrival. Nutanix revealed it had appointed Ramaswami as its CEO in late 2020, just two days after he quit his role as chief operating officer of its biggest rival, VMware.

Recent findings suggest that VMware was indignant about the manner of his departure, and responded with a lawsuit that accused Ramaswami of breaching his legal and contractual duties to the manufacturer by “secretly meeting” with Nutanix’s board to discuss taking over, while continuing to play a leading role in shaping its product and business strategy. The lawsuit was ultimately settled out of court about a year later.

Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering vital questions about its effects on mental health.
  • According to recent reports, published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition.
  • In a recent development, the findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering vital questions about its effects on mental health. A major latest study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.

According to recent reports, published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.

In a recent development, the findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.

Industry observers note that "What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," said lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an notable mental health concern that deserves attention.".

Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link.

Sources indicate that the connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults highlighted particularly elevated risks.

Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.

Recent findings suggest that the consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.

Industry observers note that yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.

Industry observers note that "Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood.".

Why Cannabis Use Disorder Matters.

The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.

In a recent development, the study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.

This distinction is key because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.

Sources indicate that the findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.

Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.

Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening.

One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.

Rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.

"Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," stated Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support.".

Industry observers note that the study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.

However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.

The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an key role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.

As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.

Said Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

In a recent development, the broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

Recent findings suggest that in the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in Upcoming York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

It has been revealed that audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

Industry observers note that in the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

According to recent reports, the marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:.

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

WebMD Ignite Healthcare Solutions Group President Ann Bilyew told Fierce Healthcare the increasing use of ChatGPT and other tools prior to care “changes where they [health systems] need to be visible.”.

“At WebMD Ignite, we’re working with OpenAI to understand what this channel adds to the investments health systems already make in search and other media,” Bilyew said. “The question we want to answer for clients is a practical one. Bilyew, who also serves as EVP of Health, added that is how the companies will “judge whether the channel earns a larger share of a health system’s budget.”.

WebMD Ignite has already begun activating campaigns, executives say, including one with a leading academic medical center involving cardiology. The initial campaign has tested creative variations, aligned messaging and more.

When it comes to protecting patient trust, Bilyew mentioned ChatGPT labels advertisements and separates them from answers.

It has been revealed that “OpenAI also sets eligibility requirements for healthcare advertisers and excludes personal health conversations from ad placements,” she said. “At WebMD Ignite, we bring experience on both sides. We understand how people look for care and how health systems communicate about the services they offer. That shapes the words we choose, the claims we make and where someone lands after clicking an ad.”.

WebMD Ignite says it works with more than 650 health systems—including 95% of the 150 largest in the U.S.—and 80% of the 20 largest payers.

#146224. Before Buying a Tiny Home on Amazon, Make Sure You Know the ABCs of ADUs

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1688 w)

Before Buying a Tiny Home on Amazon, Make Sure You Know the ABCs of ADUs

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1688 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In recent years, social media has been flooded with videos of folks who’ve purchased a tiny home or accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on Amazon.
  • Touting to have dropped anywhere between $8,000 to $50,000, these homeowners shared the process of just buying a house with the click of a button, along with whatever else ended up in their carts.
  • Sources indicate that but the reality is, Amazon actually prohibits the sale of habitable tiny homes and prefabricated dwellings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In recent years, social media has been flooded with videos of folks who’ve purchased a tiny home or accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on Amazon.

Touting to have dropped anywhere between $8,000 to $50,000, these homeowners shared the process of just buying a house with the click of a button, along with whatever else ended up in their carts.

Sources indicate that but the reality is, Amazon actually prohibits the sale of habitable tiny homes and prefabricated dwellings. Its Seller Central policy explicitly banned complete prefab homes, tiny house kits marketed as living spaces, modular and container homes, and other factory-built housing units.

Despite that, you’re likely to still find listings for tiny homes on the platform, which makes it even more imperative that you learn the ABCs of ADUs.

To begin with, ADUs are additional small housing structures built on a property that already has a main home or main structure. Tiny homes are usually freestanding, compact units typically under 400 square feet—sometimes on foundations or other times on wheels like an RV.

But in both cases, the structures are economical and effective ways to achieve additional living space.

"As urban populations swell and sustainability becomes a central focus, the ability to build smaller, energy-efficient homes with reduced environmental impact will be key," indicates Paul Dashevsky, co-CEO of Maxable, a leader in ADU planning, building, and development.

Sources indicate that but while tiny homes and ADUs may indeed be poised to make a positive impact toward solving the housing crisis, potential buyers need to know that you can't just plop one anywhere you please. Not to mention, tiny homes ordered online will probably also require hiring a contractor to help with assembly (adding to the overall cost).

With all that in mind, let's dig in to the details you must know prior to purchasing any ADU or tiny home. Because the last thing you want is to find yourself trying to return an entire house to sender.

While it can be exciting to imagine buying a "house" for $10,000 online, it's very important to not just look at the photos and think that's what will arrive. Read the fine print and all the reviews.

"Are you buying a complete tiny house that comes fully built, transported and rolled/craned into your backyard—or are you buying a bunch of parts that need to be assembled?" asks Dashevsy. "If assembly is required, make sure you first speak to a local contractor and determine the price of assembly.".

Though some of the advertisements—like this two-story foldable container home—say they only require five people to assemble it in 30-minutes, are you really going to feel confident asking a couple friends over—with the promise of pizza and beer afterward—to get the job done?

The reality is that most people—unless they're cool with an adult-sized Lego project—will need a skilled contractor to assist with a tiny home or ADU build. Dashevsky suggests looking for a licensed general contractor with ADU experience. "You can find them through referrals or on sites like GreatBuildz, Angi, or Yelp," claims Dashevsky.

As for the cost, it varies according to the type of tiny home or ADU.

"A brand upcoming ADU built on your site will greatly depend on your region and the size of the ADU, but a good range is $80,000 to $400,000," indicates Dashevsky, though assembling a prefab ADU may run less predicated on its complexity.

Before you buy a prefab ADU or tiny home, you must make sure that the city or county you live in allows for such dwellings on your property.

You can start by doing an Internet search for this information. Look for your city’s planning or building department. Most will have a website, and you can probably glean some information there.

However, if you're seriously in the ready-to-buy stage, it's probably wise to visit one of these offices in person for a consultation. Make sure they allow the kind of tiny home or ADU you're considering on your property. Also confirm where you’re allowed to install it. And ask about any necessary permits, building codes, and occupancy requirements in your area.

"Essentially, you want to know every single guideline they have for this structure," says Dashevsky. "The last thing you want is a tiny home you have to sell or return because your city wont allow it.".

Alternatively, you can hire a local architect who is experienced in ADUs—they should know all the city/county requirements for your location.

Unless you want to live in the dark with no water, you're going to need electrical and plumbing hookups for your tiny home or ADU. But some people who purchase a dwelling online neglect to consider those details in advance.

"A tiny home won’t do you much good if it isn’t connected to electrical power, water, and sewer at the very least," notes Dashevsky.

Recent findings suggest that speak with your local building department or utility providers to understand the process and costs to tie your tiny house in to municipal services. Or, if you have your own water well and septic tank, ask a contractor how much it will run to connect to these facilities.

For those who don't fully understand what this entails, connecting utilities to a tiny house or ADU is very similar to that for a normal house.

In a recent development, "You dig a trench from the location of the existing utilities—water, sewer, electrical gas—and run fresh pipes to the location of the new unit," says Dashevsky. "A general contractor can do this for you—this is not a DIY project— and it will probably cost around $10,000 to $20,000.".

If your region is prone to weather events or natural disasters, you'll want to ensure that your tiny house has been tested to withstand extreme conditions.

Industry observers note that "Is it rated to withstand snow, sleet, winds, earthquakes, hurricanes?" states Dashevsky. "There is no point spending a lot of money that gets wiped out in the first rainy season.".

What exactly are you looking for when you're assessing a tiny home or ADU for purchase? Check to see if it says it's made of fire-resistant materials or has a fire rating (the best is a Class A or 1). Also see if it lists a wind rating—the Beaufort Wind Scale is most commonly used with levels ranging from 1 (light air) to 12 (hurricane winds). Finally, look for an earthquake resistance rating (0-9, like the Richter scale) or a Seismic Building Code. All of these will help give you an idea of the quality of the unit you're considering.

If you're having the ADU or tiny home built from scratch, it's a slightly different story as your contractor will be required to make sure it's up to code.

"ADUs are built under the same guiding building code—International Residential Code (IRC)—as principal houses and don't have any less requirements for seismic/hurricane/snow or structural bracing," says Jeremy Tetreault, of Four Brothers Design + Build in Washington, D.C. "They are treated with the same level of scrutiny and energy ratings, too, so you should have nothing to worry about from a standpoint of being less equipped to withstand natural events.".

Getting insurance for your ADU or tiny home can sometimes be a hassle, so this is something to consider before buying an accessory unit.

Tiny homes—especially of the DIY or prefab variety—typically don't qualify for homeowners insurance policies. However, they may qualify for RV or mobile home insurance—especially if it's a tiny home on wheels (THOW)—as long as they meet building codes. The good news with this, however, is that you can often save 50% or more over regular homeowners insurance with a tiny home.

For people who have a tiny home on their property along with another home, or who build an ADU onto an existing home, it may be possible to insure the unit under the "other structures" portion of an existing homeowners policy.

The bottom line is you should speak with an insurance broker about what it will take to insure your ADU or tiny home since that will be an additional expense.

It has been revealed that it's easy to get sucked into the idea that an ADU or a tiny home you can purchase online is a great deal! But it's crucial to be realistic about all the additional costs. We already mentioned the possibility of needing to hire a contractor to help with construction—and maybe a plumber and an electrician to hook up the utilities. But there are some other hidden costs of which potential buyers should also be aware.

To begin with, do you need to lay a foundation for your tiny home? If it's on wheels, then you can probably get away without one. But for people looking for a more permanent smaller housing situation, turning it into a tiny home on foundation (THOF) will give the structure more stability.

It has been revealed that "Unless your tiny home is on wheels, it should sit on a concrete pad or foundation made of cement," notes Dashevsky. "A general contractor can do this for you but expect a ballpark cost of about $5,000 to $15,000.".

Also, if you purchase a home prebuilt but don't have room to roll it into the space where you blueprint to put it, you may need to pay for extra equipment. For example, if you have to "crane it in" then you need to factor in the price of hiring that service as well.

"The bottom line is that you really need to know all the costs involved, which are very likely to end up being close to double the Amazon 'price,'" claims Dashevsky.

However, as long as you know what to expect, ordering up a tiny home or ADU can be a prime way to create an affordable housing solution.
